sources.name: Design Council: Framework for Innovation (incl. the Double Diamond)
sources.license: CC BY 4.0
sources.license_evidence: https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/the-double-diamond/ (each resource page states it is licensed under CC BY 4.0; same statement on the Framework for Innovation page)
sources.version_or_date: Double Diamond launched 2004. The Framework for Innovation page gives no date in the fetched text, so the '2019 update' year in the brief is unverified. The Systemic Design Framework (separate entry) is the newer evolution.
sources.summary: The UK Design Council's model. Two diamonds alternate wide exploration with focused convergence: Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver. The Framework for Innovation wraps the diamonds with four design principles, a methods bank grouped into Explore/Shape/Build, and a culture layer (leadership and engagement). The page says the process is not linear: learning can send a team back to the start, early making can happen during discovery, and nothing is ever finished. There is no formal gate or engineering handoff; Deliver ends at small-scale tested solutions.

key_items.name: Discover (diverge)
key_items.one_line: Work out what the problem really is instead of assuming it, by spending time with the people affected.
key_items.use_when: Any task arrives framed as a solution or with an untested problem statement. Exit when there is first-hand evidence of the problem.

key_items.name: Define (converge)
key_items.one_line: Use discovery insight to reframe the challenge, often differently from how it was first posed.
key_items.use_when: Gate: a single evidence-backed challenge statement exists before any solutioning.

key_items.name: Develop (diverge)
key_items.one_line: Generate several different answers to the defined problem, borrowing ideas from elsewhere and co-designing.
key_items.use_when: Before committing to one design; pairs with exhaust-the-design-space.

key_items.name: Deliver (converge)
key_items.one_line: Test candidate solutions at small scale, drop the ones that fail and improve the ones that work.
key_items.use_when: Gate: a surviving solution with test evidence. This is the closest point to a handoff, but the framework defines no engineering handoff.

key_items.name: Non-linear loops
key_items.one_line: Learning can send you back to an earlier diamond. Early prototypes are allowed in discovery, and products keep iterating after launch.
key_items.use_when: Justifies re-entering discovery when tests falsify the problem framing.

key_items.name: Four design principles
key_items.one_line: Put people first; communicate visually and inclusively; collaborate and co-create; iterate repeatedly.
key_items.use_when: Principle-skill grounding (CC BY 4.0, so these can be quoted with attribution).

key_items.name: Methods bank: Explore / Shape / Build
key_items.one_line: Methods grouped by whether they explore challenges and needs, shape prototypes and visions, or build plans and capability.
key_items.use_when: Picking a method for the current diamond stage.

key_items.name: Culture: leadership and engagement
key_items.one_line: Leadership gives permission to experiment; engagement with deliverers, recipients and partners matters as much as ideas.
key_items.use_when: Stakeholder and sponsor framing in a design brief.

sources.name: Design Council: Systemic Design Framework and Toolkit
sources.license: CC BY 4.0
sources.license_evidence: https://www.designcouncil.org.uk/our-resources/systemic-design-framework/ (page states the Framework and Toolkit are licensed CC BY 4.0)
sources.version_or_date: Published under Design Council Strategy 2020-2024. Secondary sources date it to 2021; the year was not verified on the page itself. This is the current successor layer above the Double Diamond.
sources.summary: Design Council's newer framework for complex, cross-sector and climate-related challenges. It keeps the Double Diamond's diverge/converge premise but renames the stages Explore, Reframe, Create and Catalyse. Around them it adds four 'invisible activities' (orientation and vision setting, connections and relationships, leadership and storytelling, continuing the journey), six principles, four changemaker roles, and an 11-tool toolkit. A 'Designing for Legacy' series covers ending a project well.

key_items.name: Explore, Reframe, Create, Catalyse
key_items.one_line: Diverge/converge stages that put Catalyse (scaling and sustaining change) where the Double Diamond has Deliver.
key_items.use_when: System-level or multi-stakeholder problems rather than a single feature.

key_items.name: Invisible activities
key_items.one_line: Vision setting, relationship building, storytelling and continuation sit around the stages and are treated as design work.
key_items.use_when: Planning the work around the design itself: stakeholders, narrative, continuation after the project ends.

key_items.name: Four roles
key_items.one_line: Systems thinker, connector/convener, designer/maker, leader/storyteller.
key_items.use_when: Deciding which agent persona or reviewer lens to use at each stage.

key_items.name: Designing for Legacy
key_items.one_line: Close projects so later work can build on them instead of losing them.
key_items.use_when: Grounds session-pickup and pause-safely style handover notes.

key_items.one_line: Learn directly from the people you are designing for, in their context.

key_items.name: Ideation phase

key_items.name: Implementation phase
key_items.one_line: Final phase, where the chosen solution moves toward real-world rollout. Details of this phase were not reviewed this session.

sources.license: copyright ISO, all rights reserved (paywalled standard)
sources.version_or_date: 2019 edition (replaces 9241-210:2010). No newer edition was found as of 2026-10-15, but ISO review/confirmation status could not be read (bot challenge). Companion process standard ISO 9241-220:2019 was not reviewed.
sources.summary: The international standard for human-centred design across the whole lifecycle of interactive systems, written for people who plan and manage design. It is the only source here with conformance language (Annex B checklist). It has six principles, a planning clause that integrates HCD into the project plan, and four iterative activities: understand and specify the context of use, specify user requirements, produce design solutions, evaluate. It names the handoff explicitly (communicating the design solution to the people who will implement it) and separates user-based testing from inspection-based evaluation, which is how an agent can verify its own work without users. The text cannot be quoted; we can only cite clause numbers.

key_items.name: Principle: explicit understanding of users, tasks and environments
key_items.one_line: The design rests on documented knowledge of who uses it, for what, and where.
key_items.use_when: Gate before producing designs: does a context-of-use description exist?

key_items.name: Principle: users involved throughout
key_items.one_line: Users take part across design and development, not only at the end.

key_items.name: Principle: driven and refined by user-centred evaluation
key_items.one_line: Evaluation results steer the design.

key_items.name: Principle: the process is iterative
key_items.one_line: Activities repeat until requirements are met.

key_items.name: Principle: addresses the whole user experience
key_items.one_line: Covers the full experience, not just the UI surface.

key_items.name: Principle: multidisciplinary skills and perspectives
key_items.one_line: The team mixes disciplines.

key_items.name: Planning human-centred design
key_items.one_line: Assigns responsibility, plan content, integration with the project plan, and timing/resources.

key_items.name: Activity: understand and specify the context of use
key_items.one_line: Describe users, goals, tasks, resources and environments in enough detail to design against.

key_items.name: Activity: specify user requirements
key_items.one_line: Derive requirements from stakeholder needs, resolve trade-offs, and check the quality of the specification.

key_items.name: Activity: produce design solutions
key_items.one_line: Design tasks, interaction and UI; make solutions progressively more concrete; revise them from evaluation.

key_items.name: Handoff: communicate the design solution to implementers
key_items.one_line: An explicit clause for passing the design to the people who build it (title verified from the TOC only).

key_items.name: User-based testing vs inspection-based evaluation
key_items.one_line: Two separate evaluation routes: testing with users, and expert or criteria-based inspection.
key_items.use_when: The agent does inspection itself and leaves user-based testing as pending evidence.

key_items.name: Long-term monitoring
key_items.one_line: Evaluation continues after release.

key_items.name: Annex B conformance procedure
key_items.one_line: A checklist for assessing applicability and conformance.
key_items.use_when: Design-QA gate structure (cite, do not reproduce).

sources.summary: Lean UX applies hypothesis-driven, outcome-focused design inside agile teams. The canvas is its facilitation artifact: eight boxes that move a cross-functional team from business problem to the smallest experiment that can test the riskiest assumption. The author describes it as a way to make sure learning happens every sprint and to shift the conversation from outputs to outcomes. It has no stage gates. The 'gate' is having a falsifiable hypothesis and a chosen experiment.

key_items.name: Box 1: Business problem
key_items.one_line: What changed in the world that now needs solving.

key_items.name: Box 2: Business outcomes
key_items.one_line: A measurable change in someone's behaviour, not a feature.

key_items.name: Box 3: Users
key_items.one_line: Shared, aligned personas including admins and buyers.

key_items.name: Box 4: User outcomes and benefits
key_items.one_line: Goals, benefits and emotions users get; kept distinct from business outcomes.

key_items.name: Box 5: Solutions
key_items.one_line: A wide brainstorm, including non-technical and business-model options.

key_items.name: Box 6: Hypotheses
key_items.one_line: Link a solution and a user to a predicted outcome in a testable statement.

key_items.name: Box 7: Most important thing to learn first
key_items.one_line: Surface every discipline's risks and pick the riskiest; early on, prioritise value risk over feasibility.

key_items.name: Box 8: Least work to learn it
key_items.one_line: Design the smallest experiment that answers box 7.

key_items.name: Lean Product Canvas / Lean Strategy Canvas
key_items.one_line: The author's current replacements for the Lean UX Canvas.
key_items.use_when: Check these before building a skill on the v2 canvas.

sources.name: SVPG: Dual-Track Agile (now Continuous Discovery / Continuous Delivery), Marty Cagan
sources.license: copyright SVPG, all rights reserved
sources.version_or_date: Article 2012, updated note. Cagan retired the term 'dual-track agile' from INSPIRED v2 onward and now says continuous discovery and continuous delivery.
sources.summary: Runs discovery and delivery in parallel. Discovery quickly produces validated backlog items; delivery produces releasable software. Product manager, designer and lead engineer work side by side instead of passing artifacts down a mini-waterfall. Validation happens in discovery, usually before any production code, because building and launching is the slowest and most expensive way to test an idea. The handoff is explicit: the validated prototype becomes the spec for delivery. Cagan pairs it with Lean UX.

key_items.name: Two parallel tracks
key_items.one_line: Discovery yields validated backlog items; delivery yields releasable software. They run at the same time.
key_items.use_when: Structuring a design-mode run alongside engineering work.

key_items.name: PM + designer + lead engineer together
key_items.one_line: Collaborate on creating and validating items; no role-by-role artifact relay.
key_items.use_when: Grounds multi-lens review instead of sequential handoffs.

key_items.name: Validate before production code
key_items.one_line: Use prototypes to test ideas faster and cheaper than shipping.
key_items.use_when: Gate: no backlog item enters delivery unvalidated.

key_items.name: Prototype as spec
key_items.one_line: The validated prototype is the handoff artifact for delivery.

key_items.name: Terminology change
key_items.one_line: Cagan now prefers continuous discovery/delivery, because 'dual-track' drew too much focus to process over principles.

sources.name: Product Talk: Opportunity Solution Trees (Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits)
sources.license: copyright Product Talk; no open license found

sources.version_or_date: Article live as of 2026-10-15; the page now also covers AI-generated trees and AI evals as a discovery habit.
sources.summary: A visual discovery structure. The root is one desired outcome tied to business value. Below it sits the opportunity space (customer needs, pain points, desires), then the solution space, then assumption tests. The article sets prerequisites (a theory of the customer and value proposition, a clear outcome, and a few story-based customer interviews) and warns against inventing opportunities. Exit decisions after assumption tests are: refine an idea for delivery, or pick a new target opportunity.

key_items.name: Root: desired outcome
key_items.one_line: Start from one measurable outcome, not a feature request.

key_items.name: Opportunity space
key_items.one_line: Map customer needs, pain points and desires taken from real interviews.

key_items.name: Target one opportunity
key_items.one_line: Brainstorm solutions for one chosen opportunity, not the whole tree.

key_items.name: Assumption tests
key_items.one_line: Break solutions into underlying assumptions and test the most important first.

key_items.name: Decide next
key_items.one_line: Either refine a winning idea for delivery or switch target opportunity.

key_items.name: Prerequisites
key_items.one_line: Needs a defined outcome and a handful of story-based interviews; without real inputs the tree is not meaningful.
key_items.use_when: The agent must flag missing research instead of inventing it.

sources.name: GV Design Sprint (and Sprint book / thesprintbook.com)
sources.publisher: GV (Google Ventures); book by Jake Knapp, John Zeratsky, Braden Kowitz (now under Character Capital)
sources.license: copyright GV (2019) / Character Capital LLC; all rights reserved
sources.license_evidence: https://www.gv.com/sprint/ (footer © 2019 GV); https://www.thesprintbook.com/how (footer ©2026 Character Capital LLC)
sources.version_or_date: Book 2016. The GV page is a 2019 snapshot; the authors' current hub is thesprintbook.com. They have since added a 'Foundation Sprint' (name only; steps not reviewed).
sources.summary: A five-day, time-boxed process to answer a critical business question by prototyping and testing with customers instead of building and launching. Monday: agree a long-term goal, map the problem, ask experts, pick a target. Tuesday: review existing ideas, sketch individually. Wednesday: critique, decide, storyboard. Thursday: build a realistic customer-facing facade prototype. Friday: interview customers and watch their reactions. Pre-sprint gates: the right challenge, the right team, cleared time. The output is test data, not a build spec; handoff to engineering is implicit.

key_items.name: Set the stage
key_items.one_line: Pick a challenge worth a week, a decider and a cross-functional team, and clear the calendar.
key_items.use_when: Gate before starting a sprint-style playbook.

key_items.name: Monday: map and target
key_items.one_line: Start at the end with a long-term goal, map the challenge, gather expert input, choose a focused target.

key_items.name: Tuesday: sketch
key_items.one_line: Remix existing ideas, then each person sketches a solution independently.

key_items.name: Wednesday: decide and storyboard
key_items.one_line: Critique the sketches, pick the strongest, weave them into a storyboard.

key_items.name: Thursday: prototype
key_items.one_line: Build only the customer-facing surface: realistic, but fake underneath.

key_items.name: Friday: test
key_items.one_line: Interview customers with the prototype and summarise patterns.
key_items.use_when: Validation. The agent prepares the script and leaves the sessions to humans.

sources.name: Shape Up (Basecamp / 37signals, Ryan Singer)
sources.license: copyright 37signals LLC, all rights reserved (free to read online)
sources.license_evidence: https://basecamp.com/shapeup (footer: Copyright ©1999-2026 37signals LLC. All rights reserved.)
sources.version_or_date: Online book, live as of 2026-10-15 (now includes a 'How to implement Shape Up in Basecamp' section)
sources.summary: A product-development cycle with an explicit design-to-build handoff. Senior people 'shape' work before betting on it: they set an appetite (time budget, not an estimate), sketch solutions at low fidelity (breadboards, fat-marker sketches), and remove rabbit holes. The result is written up as a pitch. Stakeholders bet on pitches at a betting table held during a two-week cool-down. A team then builds for one six-week cycle without interruption. A circuit breaker cancels work that does not ship within the cycle. During building, the team splits work into scopes, tracks unknowns on a hill chart, and cuts scope to fit the time box.

key_items.name: Appetite
key_items.one_line: Decide how much time the problem is worth before designing, and design to fit it.
key_items.use_when: Fixed time, variable scope for any design task.

key_items.name: Shaping (breadboards, fat-marker sketches)
key_items.one_line: Define key solution elements at low fidelity: affordances and connections, no styling.
key_items.use_when: Making an abstract idea concrete enough to bet on.

key_items.name: Rabbit holes
key_items.one_line: Find and resolve the unknowns that could blow the time box before committing.

key_items.name: Pitch
key_items.one_line: Written document presenting the shaped problem, appetite and solution sketch.
key_items.use_when: Handoff artifact from design to the build team.

key_items.name: Betting table / cool-down
key_items.one_line: Pitches are chosen in a two-week cool-down between six-week cycles.

key_items.name: Circuit breaker
key_items.one_line: By default, cancel a project that does not ship in one cycle instead of extending it.
key_items.use_when: Stop rule for runaway design loops.

key_items.name: Scopes and hill charts
key_items.one_line: Split work into independently finishable scopes and show each moving from unknown (uphill) to known to done.

key_items.name: Scope hammering and nice-to-haves
key_items.one_line: Push hard on requirements to fit the time box; mark optional tasks to cut first.

sources.name: GOV.UK Service Manual: Agile delivery phases (discovery, alpha, beta, live)
sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0
sources.license_evidence: https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3/ (Service Manual footer: all content available under OGL v3.0 except where otherwise stated)
sources.version_or_date: Live pages fetched 2026-10-15 (alpha, beta and live pages updated to the current Service Standard)
sources.summary: The most fully gated lifecycle in this set, and openly licensed. Discovery (typically 4-8 weeks): understand users, constraints, policy intent and opportunities; reframe any pre-set solution as a problem; consider options that need no build; do not build. Alpha (typically 6-8 weeks): prototype and test the riskiest assumptions, keep it non-public, and throw the code away. Beta: build the chosen idea for real, first in private beta, then public beta after an assessment, with an accessibility audit fixed before going public. Live: keep improving and retire the service if it is no longer needed. Every phase has explicit exit criteria, and stopping is presented as a legitimate outcome. Engineers are inside the multidisciplinary team throughout. The real build transition is alpha to beta, and new patterns are contributed back to the GOV.UK Design System.

key_items.name: Discovery: reframe the given solution
key_items.one_line: Question any pre-defined solution and restate it as a user problem, including what is out of scope.
key_items.use_when: First step of any design task that arrives as a feature request.

key_items.name: Discovery: consider not building
key_items.one_line: Content, campaigns, partners, better staff information or open data/APIs may solve the problem more cheaply.
key_items.use_when: Before committing to a UI build.

key_items.name: Discovery exit gate
key_items.one_line: Go to alpha only if a viable, cost-effective service exists. Carry forward the wider context, a ranked list of ideas to test, a team shape and success measures.

key_items.name: Alpha: riskiest assumptions first
key_items.one_line: Prototype only enough to test the most dangerous assumptions (user, technical, legal or integration).

key_items.name: Alpha: throwaway, non-public prototypes
key_items.one_line: Build just enough to test ideas, not production code, and expect to discard it.
key_items.use_when: Stops agents from shipping prototype code.

key_items.name: Alpha exit gate
key_items.one_line: Proceed to beta only with confidence that user needs can be met cost-effectively and with budget and people (including research budget), explained against the success metrics. Otherwise stop or repeat.
key_items.use_when: Gate before handoff to engineering build.

key_items.name: Beta: private then public
key_items.one_line: Build for real, roll out to limited users, iterate, then pass an assessment to open to everyone. Keep any legacy service running.
key_items.use_when: Engineering build phase; design keeps researching and iterating.

key_items.name: Beta: accessibility gate
key_items.one_line: Run regular accessibility testing, research with disabled people, fix audit issues before public beta, and publish an accessibility statement.

key_items.name: Use and contribute to the GOV.UK Design System
key_items.one_line: Use shared styles, components and patterns, and feed new or learned patterns back.

key_items.name: Live: sustain, measure, retire
key_items.one_line: Keep iterating, check metrics tell you what you need, test changes across devices and channels, and retire the service if it is no longer needed.

key_items.name: Work in the open
key_items.one_line: Blog and run show-and-tells in every phase unless confidentiality prevents it.

sources.name: GOV.UK Service Standard (14 points)
sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0

sources.summary: Fourteen points that services are assessed against at the alpha, beta and live gates. Points 1-5 cover users and experience (understand needs, solve a whole problem, join up channels, keep it simple, make sure everyone can use it). Points 6-8 cover team and way of working (multidisciplinary, agile, iterate frequently). Points 9-14 cover security/privacy, defined success and published performance data, tool choice, open source code, open standards and common components, and reliability. It works as a ready-made design-QA and assessment rubric that can be quoted under OGL.

key_items.name: 1 Understand users and their needs
key_items.one_line: Research-based understanding of users.

key_items.name: 2 Solve a whole problem for users
key_items.one_line: Scope the service to the user's full journey across organisations.

key_items.name: 3 Joined-up experience across all channels
key_items.one_line: Online and offline parts work together.

sources.summary: A public-domain catalogue of HCD method cards in four phase categories plus Fundamentals. Discover builds understanding of the problem and people. Decide turns research into insights, checks assumptions and forms design hypotheses. Make produces testable designs. Validate tests design hypotheses with users. Each card gives what, why, time required, step-by-step how-to and 18F examples, with US-government considerations (privacy, Paperwork Reduction Act). CC0 means the text can be copied or adapted straight into skill files, which makes it the best open source for method-level leaf skills.

sources.summary: Thirteen plays drawn from private-sector and government practice. Each has a checklist and key questions, which makes it directly usable as an assessment rubric. Design-relevant plays: understand what people need (1), address the whole experience (2), make it simple and intuitive with a shared design system, the U.S. Web Design System (3), agile and iterative delivery with an MVP within three months and frequent usability tests (4), use data to drive decisions (12), and default to open (13). Plays 5-11 cover budgets/contracts, accountable leadership, teams, tech stack, hosting, automated testing and deployment, and security/privacy.

key_items.name: Play 1: Understand what people need
key_items.one_line: Research users early, test prototypes with real people, document and share findings, and keep a prioritised list of user tasks.

key_items.name: Play 2: Whole experience
key_items.one_line: Map online and offline touchpoints, rank pain points, and set per-step metrics.

key_items.name: Play 3: Simple and intuitive
key_items.one_line: Use a consistent design system (USWDS by default), show users where they are, plain language, accessibility, save-and-return.

key_items.name: Play 4: Agile and iterative
key_items.one_line: Ship an MVP that solves a core need within about three months, test usability often, release several times a month.

key_items.name: Play 12: Use data to drive decisions
key_items.one_line: Instrument the service and act on measurements.

key_items.name: Play 13: Default to open
key_items.one_line: Publish data, code and feedback channels.

key_items.name: Key questions per play
key_items.one_line: Assessment-style questions (for example, how often you test with real people).

sources.summary: An interview study of agile practitioners. Findings: agile improves transparency and predictability, but compressed timelines push teams to skip user research. Low-fidelity Lean UX artifacts (sketches, paper prototypes) are popular but often not tested with users. Stable teams matter. The main integration advice is that UX should work at least one step ahead of the development sprint and take part in planning and backlog work. It names discount usability methods as the way to keep research in short cycles.

key_items.name: Design one step ahead of the sprint
key_items.one_line: Do research and design ahead of the current sprint so developers get resolved, unambiguous work.
key_items.use_when: Scheduling design work relative to engineering.

key_items.name: Skipping research is the main failure mode
key_items.one_line: Untested designs are assumptions, and deadline pressure is the usual reason tests get skipped.
key_items.use_when: Justifies a research-pending flag instead of silent skipping.

key_items.name: Discount usability methods
key_items.one_line: Lightweight testing fits short timelines.

key_items.name: Low-fi artifacts still need testing
key_items.one_line: Sketches and paper prototypes are only useful if they reach target users.
key_items.use_when: Gate: prototype must have a test plan.

key_items.name: Team consistency and active UX participation
key_items.one_line: Stable teams learn faster; UX should take part in grooming and planning, not only receive tickets.

mapping_ideas: playbook:discovery (replaces investigation for design work): restate the requested feature as a user problem plus out-of-scope list, map constraints, list ideas that need no build, write a go/no-go memo with success measures. Grounded in GOV.UK discovery page + Double Diamond Discover/Define + 18F Discover.

playbook:alpha-prototype (replaces prototype): rank assumptions by risk, build a throwaway non-production prototype that only tests the top one, attach a test plan, and stop or loop back if it is falsified. Grounded in GOV.UK alpha + Lean UX canvas boxes 7-8 + GV Thursday facade.

playbook:shape-a-pitch (bridge from design to the feature playbook): set an appetite, breadboard or fat-marker sketch, list rabbit holes, write a pitch that becomes the engineering handoff. Grounded in Shape Up.

playbook:opportunity-mapping: build an outcome -> opportunity -> solution -> assumption-test tree, but only from real research inputs; if there are none, emit a research request instead of invented opportunities. Grounded in Product Talk OST.

playbook:design-sprint-lite: Monday map/target, Tuesday parallel independent sketches (arena), Wednesday critique and storyboard, Thursday prototype; Friday becomes a prepared interview guide handed to a human. Grounded in GV sprint.

playbook:heuristic-review: the agent runs inspection-based evaluation itself (heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthrough, interface audit) and outputs severity-ranked findings. Grounded in ISO 9241-210 7.5.5 + 18F Discover/Decide cards (CC0, copyable).

playbook:usability-validation: the agent drafts the test plan, scenarios, screener, consent form and rolling-issues-log template, then marks user validation as PENDING EVIDENCE and does not block. Grounded in 18F usability-testing card + 18F Fundamentals + ISO 7.5.4.

playbook:design-handoff (new): package the validated prototype as the spec, with states, acceptance criteria, a11y notes and design-system components used or proposed. Grounded in ISO 9241-210 7.4.5 + SVPG prototype-as-spec + Shape Up pitch + NN/g one-sprint-ahead.

playbook:service-assessment / design-qa (replaces visual-parity for process QA): score the work against the 14 Service Standard points and the USDS key questions, and output pass/fail with evidence links. Grounded in GOV.UK Service Standard (OGL) + USDS Playbook (CC0).

playbook:measure-and-iterate: define metrics before build, check instrumentation answers them, and recommend retiring the feature if it is unused. Grounded in GOV.UK live + Service Standard point 10 + USDS play 12 + ISO 7.5.6.

principle:never-fabricate-user-evidence (reconciles never-block-on-the-human): separate three evidence tiers (inspection by the agent, existing research artifacts, new user-based testing). Never invent quotes, personas or findings; record missing user evidence as a pending gate and keep moving. Grounded in ISO 7.5.4 vs 7.5.5 + OST prerequisites + NN/g research-skipping finding.

principle:reframe-the-solution-as-a-problem (grounds attack-the-premise): every incoming feature request is restated as a user problem before design starts. Grounded in GOV.UK discovery + Double Diamond Discover.

principle:consider-not-building (grounds subtract-before-you-add): list content, process, data or no-UI options before proposing screens. Grounded in GOV.UK discovery alternatives + Service Standard 'whole problem'.

principle:riskiest-assumption-first: experiments target the assumption whose failure kills the idea, value risk before feasibility early on. Grounded in GOV.UK alpha + Lean UX box 7 + OST assumption tests.

principle:diverge-then-converge: never pick a design before generating alternatives; never generate without a convergence step. Grounded in Double Diamond / Systemic Design Framework (CC BY 4.0, quotable).
principle:fixed-time-variable-scope: set an appetite and cut scope rather than extend time, with a circuit breaker on runaway loops. Grounded in Shape Up.
principle:throwaway-prototypes: prototype code never becomes production code without a deliberate rebuild in beta. Grounded in GOV.UK alpha.
principle:stopping-is-a-valid-outcome: a no-go after discovery or alpha is a success state the agent may report. Grounded in GOV.UK discovery/alpha exit sections.
principle:solve-the-whole-problem: review the full journey across channels and organisations, not one screen. Grounded in Service Standard 2-3 + USDS play 2 + ISO 5.6.
principle:design-one-step-ahead: design and research for the next increment land before engineering needs them. Grounded in NN/g + SVPG dual-track.

principle:contribute-patterns-back (grounds encode-lessons-in-structure): new or learned patterns are written back into the design system or docs. Grounded in GOV.UK beta/live + Service Standard 13 + 18F design-pattern-library card.
principle:outcomes-over-outputs (grounds outcome-oriented-execution): every design task names a behavioural outcome metric. Grounded in Lean UX canvas boxes 2/4 + OST root.

principle:inclusive-by-default: accessibility and inclusion checks at every phase (alpha plan, beta audit, live statement), not only at the end. Grounded in GOV.UK alpha/beta/live + Service Standard 5 + ISO 9241-210.

LICENSE TIERS (part a, which handbooks to reference instead of pstack's code-centric ones):
(1) Copy, adapt and ship commercially: 18F Methods (CC0, via GitHub 18F/guides); USDS Digital Services Playbook (CC0, via GitHub usds/playbook); GOV.UK Service Manual + Service Standard (OGL v3, attribution required); Design Council Double Diamond, Framework for Innovation and Systemic Design Framework (CC BY 4.0, attribution required); Australian Digital Service Standard (CC BY 4.0; criteria not retrieved). Build our principle/playbook text on these. 18F and USDS can be adapted verbatim.
(2) Non-commercial only, do not blend into MIT skill text: IDEO.org Field Guide (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0, no derivatives at all) and d.school Bootleg (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, adaptations must stay NC-SA). Link only.
(3) All rights reserved, cite clause or section and link, paraphrase only: ISO 9241-210:2019 (paywalled), SVPG, Product Talk (no open license found), GV / Character Capital Sprint, Shape Up (free to read, not open), NN/g, Lean UX book and blog. The Lean UX Canvas file license is unknown.

RECOMMENDED SPINE: use GOV.UK phases (discovery/alpha/beta/live, exit criteria, OGL) as the lifecycle backbone. Use ISO 9241-210 clause numbers as the normative citation layer (principles 5.2-5.7, activities 7.2-7.5, handoff 7.4.5, inspection vs user testing 7.5.4/7.5.5). Use 18F method cards (CC0) as leaf method skills. Use Shape Up and SVPG for the design-to-engineering handoff contract. Use the Service Standard + USDS questions as the design-QA rubric.

STATUS CHANGES OBSERVED (2026-10-15): methods.18f.gov and guides.18f.gov do not resolve, so cite GitHub 18F/guides (18F/methods archived 2024-05-31). The USDS playbook page is now branded 'U.S. DOGE Service', and its repo moved from whitehouse/playbook to usds/playbook. Lean UX Canvas v2 has been replaced by the Lean Product Canvas and Lean Strategy Canvas. Cagan has retired the term 'dual-track agile' in favour of continuous discovery/delivery. The canonical Design Sprint hub is now thesprintbook.com (GV page © 2019), and the authors also offer a 'Foundation Sprint' (named only; not reviewed). ISO 9241-210:2019 is the newest edition found, but ISO's review/confirmation status could not be read. The Design Council 'Framework for Innovation 2019' date is unverified; the Systemic Design Framework is its newer successor.

KEY DESIGN TENSION for design-mode: every framework here gates on evidence from real users, which conflicts with pstack's never-block-on-the-human. ISO's split between inspection-based evaluation and user-based testing resolves it. The agent performs inspection itself, produces research kits as handoff artifacts, and records user validation as pending evidence. It must never synthesise findings it did not observe.

HANDOFF COVERAGE: explicit handoff in ISO 7.4.5 (title only verified), SVPG (prototype as spec), Shape Up (pitch -> betting table -> six-week build), GOV.UK (alpha throwaway -> beta build; patterns back into the Design System), USDS (MVP within ~3 months), NN/g (design one sprint ahead). No handoff is defined in the Double Diamond, d.school Bootleg, IDEO Field Guide (Implementation phase details not reviewed) or the OST beyond 'refine for delivery'.

sources.summary: Popular designer-facing catalogue of 30 psychology-derived 'laws', each with takeaways, origins and further reading. Good as an index and vocabulary, but several one-line definitions repeat folk versions (Miller 7+/-2, Doherty <400 ms, Hick and Hyman described as a 1952 'team'). The plugin should link to it and restate each law in its own words with the original scope. Because of ND+NC, adapted text cannot be shipped.

key_items.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
key_items.one_line: Attractive interfaces are judged easier to use, which can hide real usability problems during testing.
key_items.use_when: Interpreting satisfaction or ease ratings from tests of polished prototypes

key_items.name: Choice Overload
key_items.one_line: Large option sets can overwhelm people. A meta-analysis finds the average effect near zero, with high variance between studies.
key_items.use_when: Deciding how many plans, filters or products to present; treat as conditional, not universal

key_items.name: Chunking
key_items.one_line: Break information into meaningful grouped units so it is easier to process and remember.
key_items.use_when: Formatting codes, numbers, long forms, dense content

key_items.name: Cognitive Bias
key_items.one_line: Systematic errors in reasoning shape how users perceive options and make decisions.
key_items.use_when: Reviewing defaults, framing and anchoring in flows; checking for manipulative use

key_items.name: Cognitive Load
key_items.one_line: The mental effort an interface demands; extraneous load should be removed.

key_items.name: Doherty Threshold
key_items.one_line: Fast system response keeps people engaged. The site's <400 ms figure is a later popularization; the 1982 source argues for sub-second response.
key_items.use_when: Setting response or feedback budgets; pair with progress indicators for longer waits

key_items.name: Fitts's Law
key_items.one_line: Time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with target size (log relation).
key_items.use_when: Sizing and placing touch or click targets and primary actions

key_items.name: Flow
key_items.one_line: A state of absorbed, energized focus that is fostered by balanced challenge and immediate feedback.
key_items.use_when: Designing tools for sustained work, games, creative apps

key_items.name: Goal-Gradient Effect
key_items.one_line: Motivation rises as people perceive they are closer to finishing.
key_items.use_when: Progress bars, multi-step checkout, onboarding checklists

key_items.name: Hick's Law
key_items.one_line: Choice reaction time rises logarithmically with the number of equally likely alternatives. In menus, visual search may dominate instead.
key_items.use_when: Time-critical choices with known options; not a general argument to cut menu length

key_items.name: Jakob's Law
key_items.one_line: Users carry expectations from the many other products they use, so follow prevailing conventions.
key_items.use_when: Choosing patterns for nav, checkout, forms, icons

key_items.name: Law of Common Region
key_items.one_line: Elements inside a shared bounded area are seen as a group.

key_items.name: Law of Proximity
key_items.one_line: Elements placed near each other are read as related.
key_items.use_when: Spacing labels and inputs, grouping form sections

key_items.name: Law of Pragnanz
key_items.one_line: Ambiguous visuals are perceived as their simplest possible form.
key_items.use_when: Icon and logo design, simplifying visual structure

key_items.name: Law of Similarity
key_items.one_line: Elements that look alike are perceived as belonging together.

key_items.name: Law of Uniform Connectedness
key_items.one_line: Elements joined by lines or shared color fields are seen as more related.

key_items.name: Mental Model
key_items.one_line: Users act on a simplified internal model of how a system works; design should match or teach it.

key_items.name: Miller's Law
key_items.one_line: The site states 7+/-2 items in working memory; current evidence (Cowan) puts central capacity near 3-5 chunks, and menus that rely on recognition are not limited by it.
key_items.use_when: Only for recall-dependent tasks; never to cap menu or nav length

key_items.name: Occam's Razor
key_items.one_line: Among equally good explanations or designs, prefer the one with the fewest assumptions or elements.
key_items.use_when: Choosing between design alternatives (aphorism, not an empirical UX law)

key_items.name: Paradox of the Active User
key_items.one_line: People start using software right away instead of reading instructions.
key_items.use_when: Placing help in context, progressive disclosure

key_items.name: Pareto Principle
key_items.one_line: A minority of causes often produce most of the effects (~80/20).
key_items.use_when: Prioritizing features or fixes (heuristic, not a law of perception)

key_items.name: Parkinson's Law
key_items.one_line: Work expands to fill the time allotted.
key_items.use_when: Timeboxing tasks, autofill to shorten forms (aphorism)

key_items.name: Peak-End Rule
key_items.one_line: People recall an experience mainly by its most intense moment and its ending.
key_items.use_when: Designing completion states, error recovery, end of flows

key_items.name: Postel's Law
key_items.one_line: Accept varied input tolerantly and emit strict output. The IETF (RFC 9413) warns that some readings harm interoperability.
key_items.use_when: Input parsing and validation (phone, dates); avoid silently accepting malformed data

key_items.name: Selective Attention
key_items.one_line: People attend only to stimuli relevant to their current goal, so off-goal content (e.g. banner-like UI) gets ignored.

key_items.name: Serial Position Effect
key_items.one_line: The first and last items in a series are remembered best.
key_items.use_when: Ordering nav items, lists, key actions

key_items.name: Tesler's Law
key_items.one_line: Every system has irreducible complexity; decide whether the system or the user carries it.
key_items.use_when: Deciding what to automate vs expose

key_items.name: Von Restorff Effect
key_items.one_line: The item that differs from its peers stands out and is remembered.
key_items.use_when: Emphasizing a primary CTA; do not rely on color alone

key_items.name: Working Memory
key_items.one_line: A small temporary store that holds and manipulates task information; offload it to the interface.
key_items.use_when: Multi-step tasks, comparison, carrying data between screens

key_items.name: Zeigarnik Effect
key_items.one_line: Unfinished or interrupted tasks are remembered better than completed ones (replication status not checked here).
key_items.use_when: Progress and continuation cues; treat as weak evidence

sources.summary: The canonical inspection checklist for heuristic evaluation. These are ten broad rules of thumb, not specific guidelines, and they are the backbone for a design-review playbook. Cite and link, credit Nielsen, and do not copy the article text.

key_items.name: Visibility of system status
key_items.one_line: Always show users what is happening, with timely feedback.
key_items.use_when: Loading, saving, async actions, state changes

key_items.name: Match between system and the real world
key_items.one_line: Use the users' words and real-world conventions, and order information naturally.

key_items.name: User control and freedom
key_items.one_line: Give a clear way out of mistaken actions: undo, cancel, back.

key_items.name: Consistency and standards
key_items.one_line: The same thing should look and behave the same way, following platform conventions.

key_items.name: Error prevention
key_items.one_line: Remove error-prone conditions or confirm before commit; distinguish slips from mistakes.
key_items.use_when: Forms, destructive actions, constraints on input

key_items.name: Recognition rather than recall
key_items.one_line: Keep options and needed information visible so users do not have to remember them.

key_items.name: Flexibility and efficiency of use
key_items.one_line: Offer accelerators for experts without burdening novices, and allow tailoring.

key_items.name: Aesthetic and minimalist design
key_items.one_line: Remove irrelevant information that competes with what matters (not a mandate for flat style).

key_items.name: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
key_items.one_line: Errors should be plain-language and precise, and should suggest a fix.

key_items.name: Help and documentation
key_items.one_line: Ideally no help is needed; when it is, make it searchable, task-focused and concrete.

sources.name: How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation (NN/g)
sources.license: all-rights-reserved (Copyright Nielsen Norman Group)
sources.version_or_date: fetched 2026-10-15
sources.summary: The step-by-step method for running an inspection. Several evaluators review the interface independently against a heuristic set, then findings are merged. It maps directly onto multi-agent independent review followed by synthesis.

key_items.name: Multiple independent evaluators
key_items.one_line: Use roughly 3-5 evaluators working independently, because any single reviewer misses issues.
key_items.use_when: Running parallel reviewer subagents before merging

key_items.name: Train on the heuristics first
key_items.one_line: Evaluators read and understand the chosen heuristic set before reviewing.
key_items.use_when: Loading the heuristic leaf skill into each reviewer

key_items.name: Scope and user context
key_items.one_line: Define what is being evaluated and for which users and tasks before starting.

key_items.name: Debrief and merge
key_items.one_line: Combine independent findings, deduplicate them and agree on priority.

sources.name: Severity Ratings for Usability Problems (Jakob Nielsen, NN/g)
sources.license: all-rights-reserved (Copyright Nielsen Norman Group)
sources.version_or_date: fetched 2026-10-15
sources.summary: A 0-4 severity scale for usability findings. Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence. It gives the agent a typed, explainable priority for each design-QA finding instead of an unranked list.

key_items.name: 0-4 severity scale
key_items.one_line: 0 = not a problem, 1 = cosmetic, 2 = minor, 3 = major, 4 = catastrophe; rate every finding.

key_items.name: Frequency
key_items.one_line: How often the problem occurs across users and tasks.

key_items.name: Impact
key_items.one_line: How hard the problem is to overcome when it does occur.

key_items.name: Persistence
key_items.one_line: Whether the problem recurs or users learn to work around it once.

sources.name: Short-Term Memory and Web Usability (NN/g)
sources.license: all-rights-reserved (Copyright Nielsen Norman Group)
sources.version_or_date: fetched 2026-10-15
sources.summary: NN/g's own correction of the Miller misuse. Short-term memory limits do not imply 7-item menus, because menus rely on recognition rather than recall. This is the anchor for a law-hygiene principle.

key_items.name: Menus are not capped at 7
key_items.one_line: Longer menus are fine, since users scan visible items rather than memorize them.
key_items.use_when: Any critique that invokes 7+/-2 against nav length

key_items.name: Offload memory to the screen
key_items.one_line: Avoid making users carry information across screens.

sources.name: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect (NN/g, Kate Moran)
sources.license: all-rights-reserved (Copyright Nielsen Norman Group)
sources.summary: Summarizes Kurosu and Kashimura (1995, 26 ATM layouts, 252 participants). Aesthetics correlated more with perceived ease of use than with measured ease, and polish can mask problems in tests. Ties to the primary papers ACM DL 10.1145/223355.223680 and Tractinsky 2000.

key_items.name: Perceived vs actual usability
key_items.one_line: Beauty inflates ratings of ease of use more than it changes measured ease of use.

key_items.name: Masking in tests
key_items.one_line: Probe behind positive comments, because attractive prototypes hide minor issues.

sources.name: The Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design (Ben Shneiderman)
sources.license: unknown (no license notice on the page; the text is from the Pearson textbook Designing the User Interface, 6th ed., 2016)
sources.publisher: Ben Shneiderman, University of Maryland (from Shneiderman, Plaisant, Cohen, Jacobs, Elmqvist, DTUI 6th ed., Pearson 2016, sec. 3.3.4)
sources.version_or_date: original list 1985; current wording 6th ed. 2016 (whether a newer edition exists was not checked)
sources.summary: Eight broadly applicable interaction rules refined over three decades. The author says they need validation and tuning per domain. Rule 8 repeats 7+/-2 as a rule of thumb, so restate it with the Cowan caveat.

key_items.name: Strive for consistency
key_items.one_line: Use the same sequences, terms and visual treatments in similar situations, with few and understandable exceptions.

key_items.name: Seek universal usability
key_items.one_line: Design for novices, experts, ages, disabilities, locales and devices.

key_items.name: Offer informative feedback
key_items.one_line: Every action gets a response scaled to how frequent and how major it is.

key_items.name: Design dialogs to yield closure
key_items.one_line: Group action sequences with a clear beginning, middle and confirmed end.

key_items.name: Prevent errors
key_items.one_line: Make serious errors impossible where you can, and give specific, local recovery when they happen.

key_items.name: Permit easy reversal of actions
key_items.one_line: Make actions undoable at sensible granularity to reduce anxiety and invite exploration.

key_items.name: Keep users in control
key_items.one_line: Avoid surprises and changes in familiar behavior; users should feel they drive the system.

key_items.name: Reduce short-term memory load
key_items.one_line: Do not make users carry information between displays (the page's 7+/-2 figure is outdated).

sources.name: The Design of Everyday Things, Revised and Expanded Edition (Don Norman)
sources.license: book: all-rights-reserved (copyright 2013 Don Norman, Basic Books; UK edition MIT Press). The jnd.org website text is CC BY-NC 4.0, which does not cover the book
sources.license_evidence: https://jnd.org/books/the-design-of-everyday-things-revised-and-expanded-edition/ (footer: 'jnd.org (c) 2023. Licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution, Non Commercial 4.0 International License')
sources.version_or_date: Revised and Expanded Edition, 2013 (adds 'signifiers'; last two chapters new); ISBN 978-0-465-05065-9
sources.summary: Defines the core interaction vocabulary: affordance as a relationship, signifier, mapping, feedback, constraints, conceptual model and discoverability. Adds the gulfs of execution and evaluation, the seven stages of action, slips vs mistakes, root-cause analysis of 'human error', and the double-diamond human-centered design process. This is the principle layer beneath most heuristics.

key_items.name: Affordance
key_items.one_line: Which actions are possible, determined jointly by an object's properties and an agent's abilities; a relationship, not a property.
key_items.use_when: Reasoning about what users can do

key_items.name: Signifier
key_items.one_line: A perceivable cue that communicates where and how to act; designers mostly add signifiers, not affordances.
key_items.use_when: Hidden gestures, flat buttons, discoverability bugs

key_items.name: Mapping
key_items.one_line: The relationship between controls and their effects; natural mappings need no labels.

key_items.name: Feedback
key_items.one_line: Immediate, informative communication of an action's result, without overloading.

key_items.name: Constraints (physical, cultural, semantic, logical)
key_items.one_line: Limit possible actions to guide correct use.
key_items.use_when: Input design, forcing functions, lock-ins and lockouts

key_items.name: Conceptual model
key_items.one_line: A simplified explanation of how the system works, conveyed through its system image.

key_items.name: Discoverability
key_items.one_line: Users can work out what actions exist and how to do them.

key_items.name: Gulfs of execution and evaluation / seven stages of action
key_items.one_line: Check both gaps: knowing what to do, and telling what happened.

key_items.name: Slips vs mistakes; human error is bad design
key_items.one_line: Classify errors and trace them to a design root cause (five whys) rather than blaming users.
key_items.use_when: Post-mortems of user errors, support tickets

key_items.name: Double Diamond / human-centered design process
key_items.one_line: Find the right problem, then the right solution: observe, ideate, prototype, test, iterate.

sources.name: A Century of Gestalt Psychology in Visual Perception I: Perceptual Grouping and Figure-Ground Organization (Wagemans et al., 2012)
sources.license: unknown (PMC author manuscript of an APA Psychological Bulletin article, 138(6):1172-1217, doi:10.1037/a0029333; no open license found)
sources.summary: Authoritative scientific review of Gestalt grouping and figure-ground principles. It separates the classical principles from those discovered later, which corrects designer blogs that present common region and uniform connectedness as original Gestalt laws. Use it to ground layout and grouping critique.

key_items.name: Proximity (classical)
key_items.one_line: Closer elements group together.

key_items.name: Similarity (classical)
key_items.one_line: Elements alike in color, shape or size group together.

key_items.name: Common fate (classical)
key_items.one_line: Elements moving together group together.

key_items.name: Good continuation (classical)
key_items.one_line: Smooth continuous contours are seen as belonging together.

key_items.name: Closure (classical)
key_items.one_line: Incomplete shapes are perceived as whole.
key_items.use_when: Icons, cropped content hinting at scroll

key_items.name: Symmetry and parallelism (classical)
key_items.one_line: Symmetric or parallel elements are grouped as one figure.

key_items.name: Synchrony (newer)
key_items.one_line: Elements changing at the same time group together.

key_items.name: Common region (newer)
key_items.one_line: Elements within a shared enclosed area group together.

key_items.name: Element and uniform connectedness (newer)
key_items.one_line: Physically connected elements group strongly.

key_items.name: Figure-ground organization
key_items.one_line: The visual system assigns which region is the object and which is background.

sources.name: Dieter Rams: Ten principles for good design (Vitsoe)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
sources.license_evidence: https://www.vitsoe.com/us/about/good-design (page footer: 'These principles can be shared accurately and fairly under the Creative Commons CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence')
sources.version_or_date: formulated late 1970s; page fetched 2026-10-15
sources.summary: Ten product-design values from Dieter Rams, published by Vitsoe. They give a quality and ethics lens (useful, understandable, honest, unobtrusive, as little design as possible) that complements usability heuristics. ND forbids shipping adapted wording, so paraphrase and link.

key_items.name: Innovative
key_items.one_line: Innovation follows new technology and is never an end in itself.

key_items.name: Makes a product useful
key_items.one_line: Serve function, psychological and aesthetic needs, and cut whatever detracts from use.

key_items.name: Aesthetic
key_items.one_line: Aesthetic quality is part of usefulness, and only well-made things are beautiful.

key_items.name: Makes a product understandable
key_items.one_line: Structure should be self-explanatory.

key_items.name: Unobtrusive
key_items.one_line: Tools stay neutral and restrained, leaving room for the user.

key_items.name: Honest
key_items.one_line: Never overstate capability or manipulate.

key_items.name: Long-lasting
key_items.one_line: Avoid fashion so the design does not date.

key_items.name: Thorough down to the last detail
key_items.one_line: Nothing arbitrary; care shows respect for users.

key_items.name: Environmentally friendly
key_items.one_line: Conserve resources and minimize visual and physical pollution over the lifecycle.

key_items.name: As little design as possible
key_items.one_line: Less but better: concentrate on essentials.

sources.name: First Principles of Interaction Design, Revised and Expanded (Bruce Tognazzini)
sources.license: copyright 1978-2014 Bruce Tognazzini; copies for personal use permitted with the notice retained; other uses need the author's permission
sources.version_or_date: 2014 revision (adds Aesthetics; restores Discoverability and Simplicity)
sources.summary: A deep, example-rich set of 19 principle categories covering GUI, web, mobile and wearables. NN/g calls it slightly too long for heuristic evaluation but a useful checklist, so use it for a deep critique pass rather than a fast inspection.

key_items.name: Aesthetics
key_items.one_line: Fashion must not beat usability; user-test visual changes like behavioral ones.

key_items.name: Anticipation
key_items.one_line: Bring the information and tools each step needs to the user.

key_items.name: Autonomy
key_items.one_line: Users own the environment within sensible bounds; keep status visible and accurate.

key_items.name: Color
key_items.one_line: Never rely on color alone, but do not strip color either.

key_items.name: Consistency
key_items.one_line: The strictness of consistency varies by level; make different things look different; aim for continuity over time; match user expectations.

key_items.name: Defaults
key_items.one_line: Defaults should be easy to replace, intelligent, and clearly scoped when reverting.

key_items.name: Discoverability
key_items.one_line: Hiding complexity tends to increase it; make controls findable.

key_items.name: Efficiency of the user
key_items.one_line: Optimize for the human's time and productivity, not the machine's.

key_items.name: Explorable interfaces
key_items.one_line: Offer safe exploration with reversible actions and stable landmarks.

key_items.name: Fitts's Law
key_items.one_line: Size and place targets by distance and size; screen edges act as large targets.

key_items.name: Human interface objects
key_items.one_line: On-screen objects should behave consistently and predictably.

key_items.name: Latency reduction
key_items.one_line: Reduce and mask waits, and give immediate acknowledgement.

key_items.name: Learnability
key_items.one_line: Minimize learning time while supporting growth to expertise.

key_items.name: Metaphors
key_items.one_line: Choose metaphors that convey the whole conceptual model.

key_items.name: Protect users' work
key_items.one_line: Never lose user work; save continuously.

key_items.name: Readability
key_items.one_line: Text must be legible in contrast and size for real eyes.

key_items.name: Simplicity
key_items.one_line: Keep it simple but not simplistic; avoid the illusion of simplicity.

key_items.name: State
key_items.one_line: Track and restore user state across sessions and devices.

key_items.name: Visible navigation
key_items.one_line: Keep navigation visible and shallow; do not make users build mental maps.

sources.name: Universal Principles of Design, Updated and Expanded Third Edition (Lidwell, Holden, Butler)
sources.license: unknown (commercial book; no open license found)
sources.version_or_date: 3rd edition (ISBN 978-0-7603-7516-7; eISBN 978-0-7603-7517-4); publication year not verified
sources.summary: Cross-disciplinary encyclopedia of 200 laws, guidelines and considerations; the 3rd edition updates existing entries and adds 75 new ones. Useful as a reference index for principle leaf skills. The table of contents was not retrieved (O'Reilly 403), so no entry list is given here; do not populate entries from memory.

key_items.name: 200 entries (75 new in 3rd ed.)
key_items.one_line: Per-principle explanation plus visual example, alphabetically organized (entry list not retrieved).
key_items.use_when: Looking up a named principle's definition before citing it

sources.name: ISO 9241-110:2020 Ergonomics of human-system interaction, Part 110: Interaction principles
sources.license: all-rights-reserved (copyright ISO 2020, copyright-protected document)
sources.version_or_date: 2nd edition 2020, replaces 2006; currency after 2020 not checked (iso.org blocked)
sources.summary: The international-standard counterpart to Nielsen's heuristics: seven interaction principles, each with design recommendations. The 2020 edition merged individualization into controllability and added user engagement. It suits regulated or enterprise contexts and serves as a second heuristic lens for a review.

key_items.name: Suitability for the user's tasks
key_items.one_line: Support task completion without unnecessary steps or information.

key_items.name: Self-descriptiveness
key_items.one_line: Capabilities and use are obvious, with information where needed.

key_items.name: Conformity with user expectations
key_items.one_line: Behavior is predictable from context and conventions.

key_items.name: Learnability
key_items.one_line: Support discovery and exploration, and help when learning is needed.

key_items.name: Controllability
key_items.one_line: The user controls pace, sequence and individualization (absorbs the old individualization principle).

key_items.name: Use error robustness
key_items.one_line: Help avoid errors, tolerate identifiable ones, and support recovery.

key_items.name: User engagement
key_items.one_line: Present functions and information in an inviting, motivating way (new in 2020).
key_items.use_when: Consumer and engagement features; check against dark patterns

sources.name: Fitts' Law (I. Scott MacKenzie, HHCI 2018 chapter; and MacKenzie 1992, Human-Computer Interaction 7:91-139)
sources.license: unknown (no license notice found on yorku.ca page)
sources.version_or_date: 2018 chapter; cites ISO 9241-9 (possibly superseded by ISO 9241-411; not checked)
sources.summary: Authoritative HCI treatment of Fitts' law. It covers Fitts' original index of difficulty, the Shannon formulation now used in HCI (which cannot go negative), effective width, and throughput as the ISO-style performance metric. The plugin should cite this formula rather than the vague 'bigger is better' version.

key_items.name: Fitts (1954) index of difficulty
key_items.one_line: ID = log2(2A/W), where A is the movement amplitude and W is the target width.

key_items.name: Shannon formulation
key_items.one_line: ID = log2(A/W + 1) and MT = a + b*ID; fits data better and is never negative.

key_items.name: Effective width
key_items.one_line: Adjust W using the observed spread of selections, so error rates are normalized.

key_items.name: Throughput
key_items.one_line: Bits per second, the main performance measure in ISO-style device evaluations.

sources.name: Selection from alphabetic and numeric menu trees using a touch screen: breadth, depth, and width (Landauer & Nachbar, CHI '85)
sources.license: unknown (ACM Digital Library; terms not fetched)
sources.summary: Classic evidence on when Hick-Hyman applies to menus. It holds for easily distinguished stimuli with arbitrary assigned responses. For menus the open question is choice vs visual scan-and-match, and the menus were ordered (alphabetic or numeric). Use it as the scope note for any Hick's-law claim.

key_items.name: Hick-Hyman scope
key_items.one_line: Log choice-time holds for easily distinguished stimuli mapped to arbitrary responses.
key_items.use_when: Before citing Hick for UI choices

key_items.name: Menus may be scan-bound
key_items.one_line: Menu selection time can be driven by visual search instead of choice.

key_items.name: Decision + movement in series
key_items.one_line: Ordered touch-menu times fit Hick-Hyman (decision) plus Fitts (movement) combined.

sources.name: On the Rate of Gain of Information (W. E. Hick, 1952)
sources.license: unknown (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 4(1):11-26; abstract via CiNii)
sources.summary: Origin of Hick's law: choice-reaction experiments with up to ten alternatives, finding a roughly constant rate of information gain (about 5 bits/s). It is a law about reacting to one of N stimuli, not about deliberating over menu content. Hyman's separate 1953 paper extended it; they were not a 1952 team, as Laws of UX implies.

key_items.name: Choice reaction time and information
key_items.one_line: Reaction time tracks the information (uncertainty) of the stimulus set, measured with up to 10 alternatives.

sources.name: The Economic Value of Rapid Response Time (Doherty & Thadhani, IBM, Nov 1982), reproduction
sources.license: unknown (blog reproduction of IBM material; original IBM report not fetched)
sources.publisher: IBM (reproduced on Jim Elliott's Mainframe Blog)
sources.version_or_date: 1982 (secondary sources cite IBM technical report GE20-0752-0; not verified)
sources.summary: Origin of the 'Doherty threshold'. The reproduced text argues for sub-second response: productivity rises more than proportionally as response time drops, with steep gains below 1 s and a data point at 0.3 s (180 vs 371 transactions per hour). '400 ms' does not appear in the text (figures not inspected). The plugin should say 'aim for sub-second; 400 ms is a later popularization'.

key_items.name: Sub-second response
key_items.one_line: Gains rise dramatically once system response falls below one second.

key_items.name: Replaces the old 2-second norm
key_items.one_line: Challenges R. B. Miller's earlier view that waits of up to 2 s were acceptable.

sources.name: The Magical Mystery Four: How is Working Memory Capacity Limited, and Why? (Nelson Cowan, 2010)
sources.license: unknown (PMC author manuscript of Current Directions in Psychological Science; no open license found)
sources.publisher: Current Directions in Psychological Science (via PMC)
sources.summary: The modern estimate of working-memory capacity: a central store of about 3-5 meaningful items in young adults, as distinct from task-dependent repetition span. Laws of UX itself links it. It replaces the folk 7+/-2 number in any plugin principle.

key_items.name: Central capacity of about 3-5 chunks
key_items.one_line: Use 3-5 meaningful items, not 7+/-2, when a design truly depends on holding things in mind.

sources.name: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd, 2010)
sources.license: unknown (abstract carries a copyright 2010 Journal of Consumer Research notice; reuse terms not found)
sources.summary: Meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 experiments (N=5,036). The mean choice-overload effect is virtually zero with large variance; no sufficient conditions were found. This is the scope note for the Choice Overload law: treat it as context-dependent.

key_items.name: Near-zero mean effect
key_items.one_line: Do not assume fewer options always help; test it in context.

sources.name: RFC 9413: Maintaining Robust Protocols (IAB)
sources.license: IETF Trust: copyright 2023, subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust Legal Provisions
sources.version_or_date: June 2023, Informational
sources.summary: The IETF's own reassessment of the robustness principle that Laws of UX presents as 'Postel's Law'. Some tolerant-acceptance interpretations damage interoperability over time. Use it as the caveat for applying Postel to input validation.

key_items.name: Robustness principle has costs
key_items.one_line: Silent leniency can entrench bad inputs; prefer clear, maintained validation with helpful errors.

mapping_ideas: new-playbook:heuristic-evaluation - router copies these steps: scope users and tasks; spawn 3-5 independent reviewer subagents, each loaded with one lens (Nielsen 10, ISO 9241-110, Shneiderman 8, Norman gulfs); each finding must cite heuristic ID plus screenshot or DOM evidence; merge and dedupe; rate 0-4 severity with a frequency/impact/persistence rationale - grounded in NN/g HE method, NN/g severity ratings, ISO 9241-110

new-principle:cite-laws-in-scope (law hygiene) - before invoking any UX law, state its original domain, measured quantity and conditions; banned folk versions: 7+/-2 menu caps (use Cowan 3-5 and recognition-vs-recall), '400 ms Doherty' (say sub-second), Hick for menu length (scan-bound per Landauer & Nachbar), choice overload as universal (meta-analytic mean ~0), Postel as blanket leniency (RFC 9413) - grounded in Cowan 2010, NN/g STM, Landauer & Nachbar 1985, Hick 1952, Scheibehenne 2010, RFC 9413

new-principle:signify-dont-just-afford - every interactive element needs a perceivable signifier and natural mapping; the agent verifies by screenshot that a first-time user could tell where and how to act - grounded in Norman DOET 2013

new-principle:close-the-gulfs - for each task step, walk the seven stages of action and record whether the gulf of execution (what can I do) and gulf of evaluation (what happened) are bridged; replaces generic outcome checks for UI - grounded in Norman DOET 2013

new-principle:design-for-reversal - prefer undo over confirmation dialogs; every destructive action gets a reversal path at sensible granularity; UI-level analogue of make-operations-idempotent - grounded in Shneiderman SG6, Nielsen H3, Tognazzini Protect Users' Work and Explorable Interfaces

new-principle:respond-within-perceptual-thresholds - immediate acknowledgement for every action, aim for sub-second completion, progress indicators beyond that; the agent measures real timings (explain-the-number) instead of asserting them; feeds playbook:perf-issue - grounded in Doherty & Thadhani 1982 original, Nielsen H1, Tognazzini Latency Reduction

new-principle:group-by-perception - audit layouts for proximity, similarity, common region and connectedness so visual grouping matches semantic grouping; extends playbook:visual-parity from pixel diff to perceptual-grouping diff - grounded in Wagemans et al. 2012, Laws of UX Gestalt entries

new-principle:as-little-design-as-possible - design-domain version of subtract-before-you-add: remove elements that do not serve the user's primary goal before adding new ones - grounded in Rams R10 and R2, Nielsen H8, Tognazzini Simplicity
new-principle:honest-design - no overstating capability or manipulative patterns; ISO 'user engagement' must not become dark patterns - grounded in Rams R6, ISO 9241-110 user engagement

new-principle:size-and-place-targets - compute Fitts ID with the Shannon formulation for primary actions and flag small or distant targets with numbers - grounded in MacKenzie (Fitts' law), Tognazzini Fitts's Law

new-principle:consistency-with-expectations - follow platform and industry conventions, make things that act differently look different, and prefer continuity over strict uniformity across releases - grounded in Nielsen H4 / Jakob's Law, Tognazzini Consistency (levels, induced inconsistency, continuity), ISO conformity with user expectations

new-playbook:design-critique - a deep pass using Tognazzini's 19 categories plus Rams' 10 as a quality lens, for when a fast HE is not enough (NN/g notes Tog's list is too long for HE but a good checklist) - grounded in askTog, Vitsoe

principle:prove-it-works (design variant) - heuristic findings are hypotheses; claims of 'usable' need user-test or analytics evidence, and aesthetic-usability means polished prototypes inflate ratings, so probe behind praise - grounded in NN/g aesthetic-usability effect, Kurosu & Kashimura 1995

principle:fix-root-causes (design variant) - treat user error as a design defect: classify slip vs mistake, run five whys to the design cause, fix the signifier, constraint or mapping - grounded in Norman DOET ch.5
angles.notes:
MISUSE CAVEATS the plugin must not repeat:
(1) Miller 7+/-2: the 1956 finding concerns absolute judgment and immediate memory span. Current central-capacity estimate is about 3-5 chunks (Cowan 2010, verified). NN/g explicitly says menus need not be capped at 7, because menus use recognition, not recall (verified). Both the Laws of UX one-liner and Shneiderman rule 8 still state 7+/-2, so do not copy either.
(2) Doherty threshold: the reproduced 1982 IBM text argues for sub-second response and contains no 400 ms threshold (jev: unsupported). Laws of UX asserts 400 ms (verified as its claim). The plugin should say 'aim for sub-second; 400 ms is a later popularization'. The venue (IBM Systems Journal vs tech report GE20-0752-0) is unverified. The author's name appears as Thadani on Laws of UX and as Thadhani in the reproduction.
(3) Hick's law: the original is choice reaction time to one of up to 10 stimuli (Hick 1952; Hyman's separate 1953 paper). It is not a law about deliberative decisions or menu length. Menu selection can be scan-bound (Landauer & Nachbar 1985). Laws of UX's framing of Hick and Hyman as a 1952 'team' is inaccurate. No exact formula is asserted here.
(4) Fitts: use the Shannon formulation MT = a + b*log2(A/W + 1) (verified), not the loose 'big buttons' version. MacKenzie cites ISO 9241-9; whether ISO 9241-411 superseded it is unchecked.
(5) Choice overload: meta-analytic mean effect is virtually zero with high variance (verified).
(6) Aesthetic-usability effect: it concerns perceived, not actual, usability (verified via NN/g).
(7) Gestalt: common region, element/uniform connectedness and synchrony are post-classical additions (verified). Laws of UX mixes them in without marking this.
(8) Pareto, Parkinson and Occam are aphorisms, not empirical UX laws; label them as such.
(9) Postel's law comes from networking. The IAB's RFC 9413 warns that tolerant acceptance can harm interoperability (verified).
(10) Zeigarnik: replication status was not researched (unchecked); treat as weak evidence.

sources.summary: The normative, testable accessibility baseline that most laws reference. It has 4 principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) with success criteria at levels A/AA/AAA. Version 2.2 adds 9 criteria to 2.1 and drops 4.1.1 Parsing as obsolete. Content that conforms to 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0. Use it as the pass/fail spine of an accessibility gate.

key_items.name: Contrast (Minimum), AA
key_items.one_line: Text and images of text need a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Large-scale text needs 3:1. Inactive, decorative and logotype text are exempt.
key_items.use_when: Choosing type and color tokens, and running visual QA on any screen

key_items.name: Non-text Contrast, AA
key_items.one_line: UI component boundaries, state indicators and meaningful graphic parts need at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.
key_items.use_when: Designing inputs, toggles, focus rings, icons, chart marks

key_items.name: Large-scale text definition
key_items.one_line: Large-scale text is at least 18pt, or 14pt bold, or an equivalent size for CJK fonts. This is the threshold that unlocks the 3:1 ratio.
key_items.use_when: Deciding whether a heading may use the lower 3:1 threshold

key_items.name: Contrast ratio and relative luminance
key_items.one_line: Ratio = (L1+0.05)/(L2+0.05), where L1 is the lighter color's luminance. L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linearized sRGB channels (divide by 12.92 at or below 0.04045, otherwise apply the 2.4-power curve). The constant was 0.03928 before May 2021, which makes no practical difference.
key_items.use_when: Computing contrast in a token linter or palette generator instead of judging by eye

key_items.name: Reflow, AA
key_items.one_line: Content must work at 320 CSS px wide (equivalent to 1280 px at 400% zoom) without two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that is inherently 2-D.
key_items.use_when: Responsive layout specs and zoom QA

key_items.name: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: A keyboard-focused item must not be fully hidden by author content such as sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets.

key_items.name: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced), AAA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: No part of the focused item may be hidden by author content.

key_items.name: Focus Appearance, AAA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: Sets minimum size and 3:1 change-of-contrast rules for the focus indicator.

key_items.name: Dragging Movements, AA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: Anything done by dragging must also work with a single pointer and no drag, unless dragging is essential.

key_items.name: Target Size (Minimum), AA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: Pointer targets must be at least 24x24 CSS px. Exceptions: spacing (24px circles do not overlap), an equivalent control, inline text, user-agent default, or essential.
key_items.use_when: Icon buttons, dense toolbars, mobile layouts

key_items.name: Consistent Help, A (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: Help mechanisms that repeat across pages must appear in the same relative order.
key_items.use_when: Global nav, footer and support placement

key_items.name: Redundant Entry, A (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: Do not make users re-enter information they already gave in the same process. Auto-populate it or let them select it, with narrow exceptions.

key_items.name: Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: No cognitive function test (memorizing, transcribing, solving puzzles) at login unless an alternative or assistance exists. Paste and password managers must work.

key_items.name: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced), AAA (new in 2.2)
key_items.one_line: A stricter version of 3.3.8 that also disallows the object- and content-recognition exceptions.

key_items.name: Parsing: obsolete and removed in 2.2
key_items.one_line: Removed because assistive technology no longer parses HTML directly. Its problems are now covered by other criteria.
key_items.use_when: Updating legacy checklists and VPAT templates

key_items.name: Name, Role, Value, A
key_items.one_line: Every UI component exposes a programmatic name, role and state to assistive technology.

sources.summary: Seven short, practitioner-written principles for designing for permanent, temporary, situational and changing disabilities. They work well as a critique rubric, and the CC BY-SA license allows adaptation with attribution and share-alike.

key_items.name: Provide comparable experience
key_items.one_line: Equivalent quality of experience no matter how people access the product.

key_items.name: Consider situation
key_items.one_line: Design for real contexts: noise, glare, one hand, low bandwidth.

key_items.name: Be consistent
key_items.one_line: Use familiar conventions consistently.

key_items.name: Give control
key_items.one_line: Let users control content, motion and timing.

key_items.name: Offer choice
key_items.one_line: Give more than one way to finish a task.

key_items.name: Prioritise content
key_items.one_line: Put core content and features first.

key_items.name: Add value
key_items.one_line: Use device features (voice, haptics, geolocation) to make tasks easier.
