sources.summary: A phase-by-phase handbook for putting accessibility into delivery: research with disabled people from discovery onward, check designs against WCAG 2.2 principles in alpha, combine automated, manual and assistive-technology testing in each iteration, get a formal audit before public beta, and keep testing once live. It sets WCAG 2.2 AA as the minimum for UK public-sector services. Service Standard point 5 makes 'everyone can use the service' an assessment gate.

key_items.name: WCAG 2.2 AA minimum and AT support
key_items.one_line: Services must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and work with common assistive technologies: screen readers, magnifiers, speech recognition.

key_items.name: Research with disabled people
key_items.one_line: Include disabled people and assistive-technology users in user research at every phase.

key_items.name: Automated + manual + AT testing
key_items.one_line: Automated tools alone miss issues, so run all three types regularly.

key_items.name: Audit before public beta
key_items.one_line: Commission a formal accessibility audit before going public.

key_items.name: Service Standard point 5
key_items.one_line: Make sure everyone can use the service, including people with low digital skills or no internet access.

sources.summary: The harmonised European ICT accessibility standard. It brings WCAG in for web (clause 9), non-web documents (clause 10) and software (clause 11), and adds functional performance statements and hardware requirements. V4.1.1 moves to WCAG 2.2, drops 4.1.1 Parsing, adds requirements for respecting user accessibility preferences, and includes an annex mapping its clauses to the European Accessibility Act. Once it is cited in the Official Journal, conforming gives a presumption of conformity with the EAA and the WAD.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 adds 9 success criteria beyond WCAG 2.1, and 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in 2.2.
claims.note: jev check on newin22.txt; quote found.

claims.claim: New WCAG 2.2 SC and levels: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA; 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) AAA; 2.4.13 Focus Appearance AAA; 2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA; 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA; 3.2.6 Consistent Help A; 3.3.7 Redundant Entry A; 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA; 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) AAA.
claims.note: Every number and level the task brief gave matches the W3C list. AccessibleEU's 'six new requirements' for EN 301 549 v4.1.1 is consistent: 6 of the 9 are A/AA.

claims.claim: SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) requires pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions for spacing, equivalent, inline, user agent control and essential.
claims.note: Also confirmed in the normative text of /TR/WCAG22/.

claims.claim: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), AA, requires at least 4.5:1 for text and images of text, and 3:1 for large-scale text.
SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, AA, requires at least 3:1 against adjacent colors for UI component and state indicators and for graphical objects needed to understand content.
WCAG contrast ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), with L1 the lighter color's relative luminance.
claims.note: jev flagged it for review because this claim bundled the luminance formula too. Re-checked as a separate claim below, which came back verified at 1.0.

claims.claim: Relative luminance (sRGB) L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B, each channel linearized as C/12.92 if C <= 0.04045 else ((C+0.055)/1.055)^2.4. The pre-May-2021 constant was 0.03928, with no practical effect.
Large-scale text = at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, or the equivalent for CJK fonts.
The current published WCAG 2.2 is the W3C Recommendation dated 12 December 2024 (a re-publication of the 5 Oct 2023 Recommendation).
WCAG 3.0 is a W3C Working Draft dated 10 September 2026, not a Recommendation.
The WCAG 3.0 Working Draft says the WCAG 3 contrast algorithm is yet to be determined.
WCAG 3 is not expected to be a completed standard for a few more years. It will not supersede WCAG 2, and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for several years after WCAG 3 is final.
APCA is the contrast algorithm adopted in the current WCAG 3.0 Working Draft.
claims.note: Negative control. The primary draft says the algorithm is undetermined. A second check against Adrian Roselli's April 2026 post (https://adrianroselli.com/2026/04/wcag3-contrast-as-of-april-2026.html) also returned contradicted at 1.0; that post documents APCA being pulled from the draft in July 2023. Do not describe APCA as 'WCAG 3'.

claims.claim: The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) applies to covered products placed on the market after 28 June 2025.
claims.note: jev review=true because the original claim also covered services, which sit in a separate paragraph. The services part was checked on its own below. Article 31 also says Member States apply the measures from 28 June 2025.

claims.claim: The EAA applies to covered services provided to consumers after 28 June 2025.
Under the EAA, microenterprises providing services are exempt from its accessibility requirements.
claims.note: Article 4(5).

claims.note: The ETSI PDF front matter confirms 'EN 301 549 V4.1.1 (2026-09) HARMONISED EUROPEAN STANDARD' and its WCAG 2.2 references. Vispero's claim of an OJ citation planned for Dec 2026 is secondary and unverified.

The Revised Section 508 Standards require electronic content and software to conform to WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA, incorporated by reference.
claims.note: Still WCAG 2.0 as of the 2026-10-15 fetch. No 2.1/2.2 refresh appears on the Access Board page.

It grants no right to make modifications or derivatives, except derivative works inside software implementations and their documentation.
claims.note: Applies to /TR/WCAG22/ and /TR/wcag-3.0/. COGA, the Maturity Model, ACT Rules, the Understanding docs and WAI pages link the W3C Software and Document License instead, which does allow modification if the notice and a change statement are included.

claims.claim: The GOV.UK Service Manual requires services to meet WCAG 2.2 AA as a minimum and to work with the most common assistive technologies.
Microsoft's Persona Spectrum maps related mismatches and motivations across permanent, temporary and situational scenarios, e.g. one arm, an arm injury, a new parent holding an infant.
Microsoft Inclusive Design's three principles are Recognize exclusion, Learn from diversity, and Solve for one, extend to many.
The ARIA APG warns that no ARIA is better than bad ARIA, and that a role is a promise of behavior.
WCAG-EM 2 was published on 23 July 2026. Unlike WCAG-EM 1 it also covers apps and other digital products, and it has 5 steps: scope, explore, sample, evaluate, report.

The APCA reference repo is copyright Andrew Somers/Myndex, all rights reserved. Use is limited to registered beta testers or personal use, and 'APCA' is a trademark restricted to compliant implementations.

The W3C Accessibility Maturity Model (Group Note, 04 November 2025) has seven dimensions: Communications, Oversight and Culture, ICT Development Life Cycle, Knowledge and Skills, Personnel, Procurement, Support.

mapping_ideas: new-playbook:a11y-design-qa - The agent runs an automated check (axe-core, citing ACT rule IDs), then manual passes on keyboard/focus order, 2.4.11 focus-not-obscured, 2.5.8 24px targets, 2.5.7 drag alternatives, reflow at 320px, and screen-reader name/role/value. It records pass/fail evidence per success criterion and never ships on automation alone. Grounded in WCAG 2.2, ACT Rules, axe-core, and the GOV.UK testing guidance.

new-principle:compute-contrast-never-eyeball - Every text/background and UI/adjacent token pair gets its ratio computed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula against 4.5:1 / 3:1 large text / 3:1 non-text, and the agent shows the number (extends principle:explain-the-number). APCA Lc may be added only as an advisory column. Grounded in WCAG 2.2 1.4.3, 1.4.11 and the relative luminance definition.

new-principle:normative-over-draft - The agent never swaps a normative pass/fail rule for a draft one. WCAG 3 WD and APCA are direction, not gates, and the agent says so when a user or tool claims otherwise. Grounded in the WCAG 3 Intro timeline and the WD editor's note on contrast.

new-principle:pin-the-conformance-target - In discovery the agent records which legal target applies: EU EAA via EN 301 549 v3.2.1 now (WCAG 2.1 AA) moving to v4.1.1 (WCAG 2.2); US federal Section 508 (WCAG 2.0 AA); UK public sector (WCAG 2.2 AA). It defaults to WCAG 2.2 AA as the superset and writes the target into the todo list. Grounded in the EAA directive, EN 301 549, Section 508, and the GOV.UK Service Manual.

new-principle:native-before-aria - When a component is specified, the agent picks the native HTML element first. If a custom widget is unavoidable, it copies the matching APG pattern's keyboard model and roles/states into the handoff spec. Grounded in APG 'No ARIA is better than bad ARIA' and 'a role is a promise'.

new-playbook:persona-spectrum-pass - In define/ideate, for each key flow the agent lists permanent/temporary/situational mismatches across touch, see, hear and speak, then generates at least one design variant per mismatch before converging (feeds principle:exhaust-the-design-space). Grounded in Microsoft Inclusive Design and the EAA 'functional limitations' recital.

new-playbook:cognitive-load-review - The agent walks each flow against the 8 COGA objectives and checks 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication and 3.2.6 Consistent Help, flagging memory-dependent steps and unclear copy. Grounded in COGA (W3C Note) and WCAG 2.2.

new-playbook:a11y-design-system-tokens - Bake accessibility into the system: a contrast matrix for every color token pair, focus-ring tokens meeting 2.4.13 guidance, 24px minimum hit areas, color-never-alone status variants, and APG keyboard specs per component. Done once at the token/component level instead of per screen. Grounded in WCAG 2.2, APG, and WAI Designing tips.

new-playbook:a11y-conformance-report - At handoff or release the agent follows WCAG-EM 2's five steps (scope, explore, sample, evaluate, report) to produce an evidence-backed conformance statement or ACR. This replaces the gate role of pstack's shipping and opening-a-pr playbooks for UI work. Grounded in WCAG-EM 2 and the Section 508 requirements.

new-playbook:inclusive-research-recruit - In discovery and test, the research plan must include disabled participants and assistive-technology users (screen reader, magnifier, speech input). If recruiting is blocked, the agent logs the gap and keeps going with proxy checks rather than waiting on a human (honors principle:never-block-on-the-human). Grounded in the GOV.UK Service Manual and Service Standard point 5.

new-playbook:a11y-maturity-retro - At the measure stage the agent scores the team on the 7 AMM dimensions with proof points and turns each recurring audit failure into a design-system rule or lint (feeds principle:encode-lessons-in-structure). Grounded in the W3C Accessibility Maturity Model.

new-playbook:a11y-design-critique - A fast pre-code critique using WAI 'Designing for Web Accessibility' tips plus the 7 Inclusive Design Principles as the rubric. Output is a findings list with criterion references. Grounded in WAI Designing tips and inclusivedesignprinciples.info (CC BY-SA, so it can be adapted with attribution).
angles.notes:
Recommendation for the plugin: reference these, do not install pstack's code-centric equivalents. Gate on WCAG 2.2 AA (Rec, 12 Dec 2024 edition). Use the Understanding docs and ACT Rules for how-to, APG for component behavior, WCAG-EM 2 (23 Jul 2026) for the report, COGA and Inclusive Design Principles for critique, and Microsoft Persona Spectrum for ideation. Use EN 301 549/EAA/508/GOV.UK only to pick the legal target.

Things that are newer than the brief assumed:
(1) WCAG 2.2 was re-published on 12 Dec 2024. Cite that date, not just Oct 2023.
(2) WCAG 3 has a 10 Sep 2026 WD with contrast still TBD.
(3) EN 301 549 V4.1.1 shipped Sep 2026 with WCAG 2.2 but is not yet cited in the OJ, so the legal EU reference is still V3.2.1 (WCAG 2.1 AA).
(4) WCAG-EM 2 (Jul 2026) now covers apps.
(5) The Accessibility Maturity Model became a Group Note on 04 Nov 2025.
(6) Section 508 is still WCAG 2.0.

Licensing guidance for writing skills:
- W3C TR specs (WCAG 2.2, WCAG 3) use the Document License, which allows no derivatives. Paraphrase and link, never vendor the text.
- COGA, AMM, ACT, Understanding docs and APG link the permissive Software and Document License, but the WAI permission page says most WAI material is under the Document License. Default to cite-and-link.
- GOV.UK is OGL v3 and can be adapted with attribution.
- Inclusive Design Principles are CC BY-SA, with the version ambiguous between 4.0 and 2.0 UK.
- Microsoft Inclusive Design and APCA are effectively all rights reserved. Link only; do not embed APCA code.
- ETSI does not allow reproduction.
- axe-core is MPL-2.0.

sources.summary: The most complete public definition of done for a design-system component. A component moves through Draft, Preview candidate, Preview and Stable, mapped to lifecycle phases. It is Stable only when the design spec, code, tests and Figma kit all meet explicit requirements. This is the best single primary source for agent-run handoff and design QA gates. Carbon also ships an MCP server so agents can read current Carbon docs, tokens, icons and code instead of relying on training data.

key_items.name: Status ladder
key_items.one_line: Draft -> Preview candidate -> Preview -> Stable. Each step requires more completeness across code, kit, docs and design.
key_items.use_when: Labelling the maturity of a component or design deliverable before handoff

key_items.name: Spec uses only system tokens
key_items.one_line: Color, type and spacing in the spec must come from existing tokens; untokenized values are defects.
key_items.use_when: Reviewing a Figma spec or generated UI for hard-coded values

key_items.name: All interaction states specified
key_items.one_line: Spec covers hover, focus, selected, disabled, read-only, error and warning states.

key_items.name: Behaviors specified
key_items.one_line: Spec annotates responsiveness, overflow/reflow, expansion and scrolling.

key_items.name: Contrast and focus flow in spec
key_items.one_line: Text 4.5:1 (disabled excepted), interactive non-text 3:1, and a documented focus order.

key_items.name: Built to spec
key_items.one_line: Every specced interaction is implemented and the build matches the spec to the pixel.

key_items.name: Code requirements
key_items.one_line: No magic numbers, parameterized strings for i18n, works down to ~320px, typed props, and codemods shipped with breaking changes.
key_items.use_when: Reviewing component code before marking it stable

key_items.name: Testing requirements
key_items.one_line: Unit coverage >=80%; at least one Percy visual-regression test on the default story; IBM Equal Access checks on default and complex states; manual JAWS/VoiceOver/NVDA pass.

key_items.name: Design-kit requirements
key_items.one_line: The Figma component follows naming and construction conventions, matches the spec, and is published to the library.

sources.summary: The vendor-neutral JSON interchange format for design tokens. Its first stable version is 2025.10, published 28 Oct 2025. The header labels it a Final Community Group Report. The status section says it was published as a Candidate Recommendation, intended for implementation and considered stable, and it is explicitly not a W3C Standard or on the Standards Track. The release has three modules: Format, Color and Resolver (theming and modes). No newer stable version was found as of 2026-10-15; a drafts track exists. Style Dictionary, Tokens Studio and Terrazzo are reference implementations, and Figma, Penpot and Sketch support it or are implementing it.

key_items.use_when: Validating exported or hand-written token files

key_items.name: Groups, type inheritance, $extends
key_items.one_line: Groups nest tokens, pass $type down, and can extend other groups; extension cycles are errors.

key_items.name: Aliases

key_items.name: File conventions

key_items.name: Color and Resolver modules
key_items.one_line: Modern color spaces (e.g., Display P3, OKLCH), plus a resolver for themes and modes without duplicating files.

sources.summary: A living, agent-oriented ruleset for web UI quality, mostly framework-agnostic with some React/Next.js items, also published at vercel.com/design/guidelines. The README covers Interactions, Animations, Layout, Content, Forms, Performance, Design and Copywriting. AGENTS.md restates it as terse MUST/SHOULD/NEVER rules. command.md is a review command that reads files and reports violations. Caution: the README offers a viewport maximum-scale workaround for iOS input zoom, but AGENTS.md has a NEVER rule against disabling zoom that way. Ground principles in the AGENTS.md rule.

key_items.name: Keyboard and focus
key_items.one_line: Full keyboard support per WAI-ARIA APG; visible :focus-visible rings never covered by sticky UI; no outline removal without a replacement.
key_items.use_when: Implementation review of any interactive UI

key_items.name: Hit targets
key_items.one_line: Hit area >=24px (>=44px on mobile), expanded when the visual is smaller; mobile inputs >=16px to avoid iOS zoom.

key_items.name: Never disable zoom
key_items.one_line: No user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 (AGENTS.md rule).

key_items.name: Motion rules
key_items.one_line: Honor prefers-reduced-motion; animate transform/opacity; never transition all; animations interruptible.

key_items.name: URL as state
key_items.one_line: Deep-link filters, tabs, pagination and expanded panels so share, refresh and back/forward work.

key_items.name: Loading and optimistic UI
key_items.one_line: Keep button labels while loading; delay and minimum-duration loaders to avoid flicker; roll back or offer undo when optimistic updates fail.

key_items.name: Forms
key_items.one_line: Never block paste; validate after typing; inline errors with focus moved to the first error; correct autocomplete/type/inputmode.

key_items.name: Destructive actions
key_items.one_line: Require confirmation or provide undo with a safe window.

key_items.name: Review command
key_items.one_line: /web-interface-guidelines (install.sh) checks files against the rules and outputs findings by file:line.

sources.summary: Apple's platform guidance for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS. The accessibility page gives per-platform control sizes, a contrast table based on WCAG AA, text enlargement targets, and expectations for Reduce Motion and VoiceOver. An agent should check native-app designs against the platform's own conventions rather than web heuristics. Unlike the Apache/MIT/CC0/OGL sources here, HIG cannot be installed or vendored.

key_items.name: Control sizes per platform
key_items.one_line: Default/minimum: iOS & iPadOS 44x44/28x28 pt; macOS 28x28/20x20; tvOS 66x66/56x56; visionOS 60x60/28x28; watchOS 44x44/28x28.

key_items.name: Contrast table
key_items.one_line: Text up to 17 pt needs 4.5:1; 18 pt and larger, or bold, needs 3:1; offer a higher-contrast scheme under Increase Contrast.

key_items.name: Text enlargement
key_items.one_line: Let people enlarge text at least 200% (140% on watchOS), ideally via Dynamic Type.

key_items.name: Reduce Motion
key_items.one_line: When the setting is on, reduce automatic, repetitive, zooming and peripheral motion.

key_items.name: VoiceOver and color independence
key_items.one_line: Describe UI for VoiceOver and pair color with another indicator.

sources.license: Guideline text on m3.material.io: unknown (no license found). Material component code, e.g. material-web: Apache-2.0.
sources.summary: Google's open-source design system: tokens, components and foundations. The 2025 Expressive update was followed at I/O 2026 (2026-05-19) by an Expressive layout scaffold, a spacing system on an 8dp scale, watch and XR guidance, and Compose-first Android. The accessibility foundations give concrete, checkable target-size and structure rules.

key_items.name: Touch target
key_items.one_line: At least 48x48dp (~9mm), even when the icon is visually 24dp.

key_items.name: Pointer target
key_items.one_line: At least 44x44dp for mouse or stylus.

key_items.name: Target spacing
key_items.one_line: Separate targets by about 8dp or more.

key_items.name: Landmarks and headings
key_items.one_line: Map layout regions to the 8 ARIA landmark roles; label repeated landmarks without repeating the role name.

key_items.name: Reading order follows hierarchy
key_items.one_line: Designers and developers agree the DOM order matches the intended visual reading order.

key_items.name: Spacing system (I/O 2026)
key_items.one_line: Spacing tokens on an 8dp scale applied to margins, padding and gaps so layouts adapt across devices.

sources.summary: Microsoft's cross-platform system (web React and Web Components, iOS, Android, Windows). Its two-layer token model is a clear template for agent token checks: global tokens hold raw values, and alias tokens add meaning and are named by function. Alias tokens support light, dark, high-contrast and brand theming. Figma UI kits are positioned for handoff, and the site offers annotation tools for focus order and a contrast checker.

key_items.name: Global tokens
key_items.one_line: Context-free raw values for color, type, radius, stroke and motion.

key_items.name: Alias tokens named by function
key_items.one_line: A semantic layer over globals; components should consume aliases, not globals or raw values.

key_items.name: Theming via tokens
key_items.one_line: Light, dark, high-contrast and branded themes switch through tokens while keeping contrast.

key_items.name: Focus-order annotation and contrast tools
key_items.one_line: Annotate tab/focus order in the design before handoff.

sources.name: GOV.UK Design System
sources.license: Content: Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated (Crown copyright). Code (govuk-frontend, govuk-design-system): MIT.
sources.summary: An evidence-led public-sector system: components and patterns get in only with evidence that they meet user needs. The contribution criteria (useful, unique, usable, consistent, versatile) work as a gate an agent can apply before adding any new component to a design system. The proposal step asks for evidence of the user need rather than early design or code.

key_items.name: Useful
key_items.one_line: Evidence that many teams or services would use it, e.g. existing implementations.

key_items.name: Unique
key_items.one_line: Doesn't duplicate an existing component; a replacement must show evidence it's better.
key_items.use_when: Before adding or forking a component

key_items.name: Usable, consistent, versatile
key_items.one_line: Shown to work for users, aligned with existing styles, and adaptable across contexts.

key_items.name: Evidence of need before design or code
key_items.one_line: Proposals present the user need and examples in use, not a polished design.

sources.name: U.S. Web Design System (USWDS)
sources.license: Public domain in the U.S. plus CC0 1.0 worldwide (site and code). Exceptions: bundled fonts under SIL OFL 1.1 and Material icons under Apache-2.0.
sources.summary: The U.S. federal design system (v3.14.0 download on the home page as read). Two things to reuse: five design principles that act as an evaluative lens, and a maturity model in which teams adopt principles first, then UX guidance, then code (tokens + components). Everything is public domain/CC0 apart from the listed font and icon exceptions, so text can be adapted directly into skills.

key_items.name: Design principles
key_items.one_line: Start with real user needs; earn trust; embrace accessibility; promote continuity; listen.

key_items.name: Maturity model
key_items.one_line: Level 1 integrate principles -> Level 2 follow UX guidance -> Level 3 use USWDS code.

key_items.name: Tokens for color, spacing, type
key_items.one_line: Use design tokens in stylesheets; build missing components from tokens and contribute them back with research.

sources.name: Atomic Design (Brad Frost, free online book)
sources.license: Copyright 2016 Brad Frost; free to read online, no open license observed
sources.summary: A mental model for building UI as a hierarchy: atoms combine into molecules, molecules into organisms, organisms are placed in templates, and pages are templates filled with real content. For an agent, the useful part is the template/page split. Templates show content structure; pages stress-test the system with real, representative content (long names, missing images and so on).

key_items.name: Atoms -> molecules -> organisms
key_items.one_line: Compose small single-purpose elements into reusable groups and then into distinct interface sections.

key_items.name: Templates
key_items.one_line: Page-level layouts that show content structure with placeholders.

key_items.name: Pages
key_items.one_line: Templates filled with real, representative content to test whether the system holds up.
key_items.use_when: Validating designs against real data before handoff

sources.version_or_date: 2016 (online edition)
sources.install_hint: Link and paraphrase only

sources.name: The UI Stack (Scott Hurff): ideal, empty, error, partial, loading states
sources.license: Copyright Scott Hurff (2026 footer); no open license
sources.summary: Any screen can be in up to five states, and designers usually ship only the ideal one. As a handoff and QA checklist: design the ideal state first, then deliberately design empty (first-run/onboarding), partial (sparse data), error (including combined failures) and loading (expectation-setting) states.

key_items.name: Ideal state
key_items.one_line: The fully populated target; design it first and let the other states lead toward it.

key_items.name: Empty state
key_items.one_line: First impression and onboarding, prompting the first action.

key_items.name: Partial state
key_items.one_line: Sparse data (one row, half-filled profile) still looks intentional.

key_items.name: Error state
key_items.one_line: Covers invalid input, connectivity and permission failures, including combinations.
key_items.use_when: Every screen that touches data or network

key_items.name: Loading state
key_items.one_line: Sets expectations while data loads or screens transition.

sources.name: Refactoring UI (Adam Wathan & Steve Schoger)
sources.license: Commercial book, Copyright 2026 The UI Company Inc. (bundled icons have their own license)
sources.summary: Paid book (218-page PDF) of concrete visual-design tactics for developers. The chapter list doubles as a checklist of visual-polish heuristics an agent can apply in design QA: hierarchy, spacing/type/color systems, depth, images and finishing touches. Cite and link only; don't reproduce.

key_items.name: Start with a feature, not a layout
key_items.one_line: Design the core functionality before the shell; leave detail for later.

key_items.name: Limit choices with systems
key_items.one_line: Set spacing/sizing, type-scale and color-shade systems up front instead of picking values ad hoc.
key_items.use_when: Before visual design; maps to tokens

key_items.name: Hierarchy by de-emphasis
key_items.one_line: Use weight and color, not just size; de-emphasize secondary content; avoid grey text on colored backgrounds.

key_items.name: Don't rely on color alone
key_items.one_line: Accessible doesn't have to mean ugly; pair color with other cues.

key_items.name: Depth via light source and shadows
key_items.one_line: Use consistent shadows to convey elevation; use fewer borders.

key_items.name: Don't overlook empty states
key_items.one_line: Empty states deserve real design.

sources.name: Object-Oriented UX (OOUX) and the ORCA process (Sophia Prater)
sources.license: unknown (no license or copyright statement found in fetched ooux.com text). The 2015 A List Apart article is Copyright 1998-2026 A List Apart & Our Authors.
sources.summary: A structure-first method: identify the system's objects (the nouns users think in) before designing screens or flows. ORCA works through Objects, Relationships, CTAs and Attributes, from object discovery through attribute prioritization to sketching, prototyping and testing. Object discovery starts by extracting recurring nouns from briefs and research.

key_items.name: Objects first
key_items.one_line: Separate real-world things from the screens that describe them, and model the things before the screens.

key_items.name: Object discovery from nouns
key_items.one_line: Highlight recurring nouns in briefs and research to find candidate objects.

key_items.name: ORCA
key_items.one_line: For each object, define its relationships to other objects, the calls-to-action on it, and its attributes, then prioritize attributes.
key_items.use_when: Turning research into IA and navigation

sources.name: Figma Dev Mode (handoff surface)
sources.license: Proprietary documentation; Figma Terms of Service reserve all rights in the Services
sources.summary: The de facto handoff surface. Designers mark frames, components or sections as ready for dev, and Dev Mode lists those items with statuses and annotations. Developers inspect specs and component info, compare changes against version history, download assets, and use codegen or the VS Code extension. For an agent: implement only what is marked ready, pull variables and screenshots through the Figma MCP, and diff against versions to scope changes.

key_items.name: Ready-for-dev status
key_items.one_line: Only build from frames or sections marked ready; Dev Mode lists them and prioritizes sections.

key_items.name: Annotations and statuses
key_items.one_line: Designers attach measurements and notes; developers review them in Dev Mode.

key_items.name: Inspect panel
key_items.one_line: Layer type, specs, component info and last-updated time for the selection.

key_items.name: Compare changes / version history
key_items.one_line: Inspect what changed between versions before re-implementing.

sources.name: Playwright visual comparisons (toHaveScreenshot)
sources.license: Apache-2.0 (microsoft/playwright repo, which includes the docs)
sources.summary: A primary-source pixel-diff mechanism for design QA. The first run writes reference screenshots; later runs compare against them. Baselines are per browser and platform, and the docs warn that rendering varies with OS, hardware and headless mode, so baselines must be generated and compared in the same environment. This lets an agent show visual parity with evidence instead of claiming it.

key_items.name: Baseline on first run
key_items.one_line: toHaveScreenshot() writes a reference image first, then diffs later runs against it.

key_items.name: Per-browser/platform snapshots
key_items.one_line: Snapshot names carry browser and platform because rendering and fonts differ.

key_items.name: Same-environment rule
key_items.one_line: Generate and compare baselines in the same environment (e.g., CI container) to avoid false diffs.
key_items.use_when: Setting up visual regression in CI

mapping_ideas: playbook:design-qa - drive the built UI in a browser, capture Playwright toHaveScreenshot baselines per state and viewport, diff them against Figma screenshots, and run accessibility checks before reporting parity with evidence - grounded in Carbon component checklist (VRT/AVT/screen-reader/built-to-spec) + Playwright visual comparisons; replaces/extends pstack playbook:visual-parity

playbook:design-handoff - before writing code, confirm the frame is ready-for-dev, then extract tokens and variables, the state matrix (hover/focus/selected/disabled/read-only/error/warning), behaviors (overflow, responsive, scroll), focus order and landmarks. Record anything missing as a gap and proceed on a stated assumption instead of blocking - grounded in Carbon design-spec requirements + Figma Dev Mode + M3 landmarks/reading order + Fluent focus-order annotations

playbook:state-coverage-audit - for every screen, enumerate ideal/empty/partial/error/loading and prove each one renders (story or screenshot per state) - grounded in Hurff's UI Stack + Refactoring UI's empty-states chapter

playbook:token-pipeline - parse and validate token files against the DTCG 2025.10 Format module (types, aliases, no cycles, .tokens.json), check that components consume semantic/alias tokens rather than primitives, and build per-platform outputs - grounded in DTCG 2025.10 + Fluent global/alias model + USWDS tokens

playbook:component-contribution - before adding a component, require evidence it is useful, unique, usable, consistent and versatile. Default to reusing an existing component and log the decision - grounded in GOV.UK contribution criteria; pairs with pstack principle:subtract-before-you-add
playbook:component-definition-of-done - move a component through Draft -> Preview -> Stable only when the spec, code, tests and Figma kit checklists pass - grounded in Carbon component checklist

playbook:platform-conformance-review - pick the target platform's guideline (HIG for Apple, M3 for Android/web-Material, Fluent for Microsoft) and check target sizes, contrast tables, text scaling and reduced motion against that platform's numbers - grounded in Apple HIG accessibility + M3 target sizes

playbook:ui-implementation-review - run Vercel's AGENTS.md MUST/SHOULD/NEVER rules over changed UI files and report findings by file:line - grounded in vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines (MIT); replaces pstack's code-centric review for UI diffs

playbook:object-mapping - in the define phase, extract recurring nouns from briefs and research into objects, map relationships, CTAs and prioritized attributes, then derive navigation and screens - grounded in OOUX/ORCA; analogue of pstack principle:model-the-domain

principle:tokens-not-magic-numbers - every color, type, spacing, radius and motion value in a spec or code must resolve to a token; a raw value counts as a defect - grounded in Carbon (spec + code), DTCG, Fluent, USWDS
principle:design-every-state - a screen isn't designed until all five UI-stack states and all interaction states are specified - grounded in Hurff + Carbon interaction-state requirement

principle:respect-platform-conventions - use the host platform's own guideline and numbers (e.g., 44pt iOS vs 48dp Material vs 24/44px web) rather than one universal rule - grounded in Apple HIG, M3, Vercel WIG

principle:pages-test-templates - validate layouts with real, representative content (long strings, missing images, sparse data) before handoff - grounded in Atomic Design (pages stage) + UI Stack partial state

principle:evidence-before-component - new design-system additions need evidence of user need first - grounded in GOV.UK criteria + USWDS 'start with real user needs'; extends pstack principle:attack-the-premise

principle:prove-visual-parity - claims of 'matches design' need a pixel diff or screenshot pair produced in a fixed environment - grounded in Playwright same-environment warning + Carbon built-to-spec; specialises pstack principle:prove-it-works

install-vs-link policy - vendor CC0/OGL/MIT/Apache sources (USWDS, GOV.UK, Vercel WIG, Carbon, Playwright docs) as reference files with attribution. Link-and-paraphrase-only for Apple HIG (copyright plus anti-scraping terms), Refactoring UI, Atomic Design, Hurff, OOUX, and unknown-license M3 guideline text and Design System Checklist
angles.notes:
Working files (primary source text, used for jev): <local-scratch> (e.g. carbon_checklist.txt, dtcg_format.txt, hig_a11y.txt, m3_targets.txt [hand-transcribed from wigolo], wig_agents.md, hurff.txt, atomic_ch2.txt, uswdssite_LICENSE, jev_results.txt).

Load-bearing findings:
- **DTCG 2025.10 is the current stable version as of 2026-10-15.** Header: Final Community Group Report. Status section: published as a Candidate Recommendation and considered stable. Not a W3C Standard. Modules: Format, Color, Resolver.
- **Carbon's component checklist is the strongest primary source for handoff and design QA.** Carbon also ships an MCP server, worth recommending for Carbon shops.
- **Vercel WIG is the only agent-native ruleset.** MIT; AGENTS.md uses MUST/SHOULD/NEVER. Its README conflicts with AGENTS.md on maximum-scale=1; follow AGENTS.md.
- **Apple HIG can't be vendored or scraped.** It is copyrighted, and Apple's site terms ban robots, spiders and page-scraping, so link and paraphrase only.
- **Material 3 guideline text license is unknown.** Only the code (material-web) is confirmed Apache-2.0.
- **Fluent 2:** code is MIT. The site content falls under the Microsoft Terms of Use (exact clause unread because the page was blocked).
- **No authoritative, vendor-neutral source exists for redlines or design QA.** Vendor blogs were dropped. Design QA is grounded in Carbon plus Playwright instead.

sources.name: A Mathematical Model of the Finding of Usability Problems (Nielsen & Landauer, INTERCHI '93)
sources.license: copyright ACM, all rights reserved (standard ACM proceedings copyright; PDF not fetchable here, so the license line was not read directly)
sources.license_evidence: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/169059.169166 (ACM DL record; the PDF was challenge-blocked)
sources.summary: The origin of the 5-user rule. The paper models problem discovery as a Poisson process across 11 studies of user testing and heuristic evaluation: problems found = N(1-(1-λ)^n), where λ is the chance that one user or evaluator hits an average problem. Across those projects the mean λ was about .31. The paper's purpose is cost-benefit planning of how much evaluation to buy. It is not a universal constant.

key_items.name: Discovery curve
key_items.one_line: Problems found grows as N(1-(1-λ)^n) and shows diminishing returns per extra participant or evaluator.
key_items.use_when: Planning how many sessions or evaluators an iteration needs.

key_items.name: λ is project-specific
key_items.one_line: The mean λ ≈ .31 is an average across 11 studies. Nielsen's own Guerrilla HCI case fitted λ = .26, so estimate λ from your own early sessions.
key_items.use_when: Before quoting any '% of problems found' figure.

key_items.name: Applies to user tests and heuristic evaluators
key_items.one_line: The same model covers test participants and inspection evaluators, which is why the 3-5 evaluator advice comes from the same math.

sources.name: NN/g usability-testing sample-size guidance (5 users qualitative; 40 quantitative; how many test users)
sources.version_or_date: 5-user article 2000; quantitative 20-user article 2006; current quantitative summary recommends 40 (summary-quant-sample-sizes); accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: copyright Nielsen Norman Group, all rights reserved. Linking is encouraged and short quotes are allowed without permission.
sources.summary: NN/g's practitioner reading of the Nielsen-Landauer curve. Run small qualitative rounds of about 5 users and iterate: three rounds of 5 beat one round of 15, because each redesign must itself be re-tested. Covering all problems needs about 15 users. The math only holds for one homogeneous user group, so distinct groups each get their own participants. Quantitative metrics need far larger samples: NN/g recommended 20 in 2006 and now recommends 40, sized for roughly a 15% margin of error at 95% confidence.

key_items.name: Small, iterative qualitative rounds
key_items.one_line: Use about 5 participants per round and spend the budget on several rounds, not one big study.
key_items.use_when: Formative testing of prototypes or builds.

key_items.name: Per-group quotas
key_items.one_line: For two distinct user groups, use 3-4 per group. For three or more groups, use at least 3 per group.
key_items.use_when: Personas or segments that behave differently, such as parents vs children or buyers vs sellers.

key_items.name: Full coverage needs ~15
key_items.one_line: Finding essentially all problems needs about 15 users, which is why 5 is framed as the optimal round size, not as complete coverage.

key_items.name: Quantitative studies: 40
key_items.one_line: Benchmark metrics such as success rate, time and SUS need about 40 participants for a usable margin of error. The 2006 advice was 20.
key_items.use_when: Any study whose output is a number or a comparison.

key_items.name: Method-specific sizes
key_items.one_line: Card sorting needs about 15 users per group. Stable eyetracking heatmaps need about 39.
key_items.use_when: Choosing sample size for non-usability-test methods.

key_items.name: A metric needs a comparison
key_items.one_line: A usability number means something only when compared with an earlier version, a competitor or a benchmark.

sources.name: Beyond the five-user assumption: Benefits of increased sample sizes in usability testing (Faulkner 2003)
sources.publisher: Behavior Research Methods, Instruments, & Computers 35(3):369-378 (Psychonomic Society / Springer)
sources.license: unknown (journal article; the publisher's terms page was not fetched)
sources.summary: An empirical counterweight to the 5-user rule. With 60 participants tested, random subsets of 5 found as few as about 55% or as many as about 99% of the known problems. Any single 5-person sample can therefore miss nearly half the issues, and each added user markedly raises the odds of finding them.

key_items.name: Sample-to-sample variance
key_items.one_line: The 85% figure is an average. Individual 5-user samples ranged from about 55% to about 99%.
key_items.use_when: Reporting coverage claims from a single small round.

key_items.name: Diminishing but real gains
key_items.one_line: Each added participant reduces the risk of missing important problems, so add participants when the cost of a miss is high.

sources.name: Testing web sites: five users is nowhere near enough (Spool & Schroeder, CHI '01 EA)
sources.license: unknown (ACM DL record; the PDF and its copyright line could not be fetched)
sources.summary: An observational study of one task across 49 users on four production websites. Each site would have needed considerably more than 5 users to reach 85% discovery, because large, open-ended web tasks have low per-user detection rates. It is the classic evidence that λ depends on the product and the task.

key_items.name: Low detection rates on complex web tasks
key_items.one_line: Open-ended tasks on large sites push λ well below .31, so 5 users cover far less.
key_items.use_when: Testing e-commerce, search or content-heavy sites.

key_items.name: Estimate λ from your own data
key_items.one_line: Track new-problem discovery per session and stop when the curve flattens. Do not fix the number in advance.
key_items.use_when: Deciding whether to run another round.

sources.name: NN/g heuristic evaluation method (how to conduct; theory; severity ratings; 10 usability heuristics)
sources.version_or_date: How-to article 2023 (Moran & Gordon); theory and severity articles 1994; 10 heuristics 1994, updated with more explanation in 2020, heuristics themselves unchanged
sources.license: copyright Nielsen Norman Group, all rights reserved. Linking and short quotes are allowed.
sources.summary: The canonical inspection method. 3-5 evaluators each review the interface alone against a heuristic set (usually Nielsen's 10), in a narrow scope (one task, user group or device) and a 1-2 hour timebox, then consolidate findings. Severity is rated afterwards by each evaluator independently on a 0-4 scale combining frequency, impact and persistence (plus market impact), and the ratings are averaged because one evaluator's severity is unreliable. NN/g states plainly that heuristic evaluation complements user research but cannot replace it.

key_items.name: 3-5 independent evaluators
key_items.one_line: A single evaluator found only about 35% of problems on average. Aggregating 3-5 independent passes catches much more.

key_items.name: No peeking before consolidation
key_items.one_line: Evaluators must not see each other's notes until their own pass is done, or the passes stop being independent.
key_items.use_when: Running reviews in a shared doc or board.

key_items.name: Narrow scope, two passes
key_items.one_line: First walk the task to learn the product, then walk it again to log violations against specific heuristics.

key_items.name: Severity 0-4
key_items.one_line: The scale runs 0 (not a problem), 1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major and 4 catastrophe (must fix before release).
key_items.use_when: Prioritizing a findings list and making release go/no-go calls.

key_items.name: Severity = frequency × impact × persistence
key_items.one_line: Rate how often a problem occurs, how hard it is to overcome and whether it recurs, plus market impact. Combine these into one rating.

key_items.name: Average three raters
key_items.one_line: Collect severity ratings separately, after the evaluation session, and use the mean of about 3 evaluators.

key_items.name: Inspection is not validation
key_items.one_line: Heuristic findings predict likely issues. Testing with real users is still required.
key_items.use_when: Anyone proposes shipping on expert review alone.

sources.name: NN/g cognitive walkthrough (based on Wharton, Rieman, Lewis & Polson 1994, 'The Cognitive Walkthrough Method: A Practitioner's Guide')
sources.publisher: Nielsen Norman Group (method origin: University of Colorado; published in Nielsen & Mack, Usability Inspection Methods, Wiley 1994)
sources.version_or_date: Method 1990-1994; NN/g article accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: copyright Nielsen Norman Group, all rights reserved
sources.summary: A task-based inspection focused on learnability for first-time users. A cross-functional team walks the correct action sequence step by step and answers four fixed questions at each step, while a recorder logs answers. If any answer is no, the step fails. It complements heuristic evaluation: heuristics catch general violations, and the walkthrough catches places where a new user would not know what to do next.

key_items.name: Goal formation
key_items.one_line: Would users even try to achieve this step's result, that is, do they understand it is needed for their goal?
key_items.use_when: Every step of the happy path.

key_items.name: Action visibility
key_items.one_line: Would users notice that the correct control or action is available?

key_items.name: Action-goal mapping
key_items.one_line: Would users connect that action with the outcome they want?

key_items.name: Feedback
key_items.one_line: After acting, would users see that they made progress and that the action was right?
key_items.use_when: Async actions, silent saves, multi-step forms.

key_items.name: Any no = step fails
key_items.one_line: The recorder marks a step as failed if any question is answered no, which gives a pass/fail trace per task.
key_items.use_when: Producing an evidence log for onboarding flows.

sources.name: NN/g research-method guidance: thinking aloud, triangulation, and choosing UX research methods
sources.version_or_date: Think-aloud 2012; triangulation and method-landscape articles accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: copyright Nielsen Norman Group, all rights reserved
sources.summary: Think-aloud testing asks participants to keep verbalizing what they look at, try and think while using the system. Nielsen calls it possibly the single most valuable usability method, and it suits Agile cadences. The triangulation article defines the practice of using several data sources or analysis methods to raise a finding's credibility, especially pairing attitudinal with behavioral data and qualitative with quantitative. The method-landscape article (which-ux-research-methods) maps methods by attitudinal/behavioral and qual/quant axes.

key_items.name: Think-aloud protocol
key_items.one_line: Participants narrate continuously while doing real tasks, and the facilitator stays neutral and avoids leading.

key_items.name: Triangulation
key_items.one_line: Confirm a finding through at least one independent source or method before treating it as established.
key_items.use_when: A single study or metric is about to drive a big decision.

key_items.name: Method landscape
key_items.one_line: Pick methods by question type: what people do (behavioral) vs say (attitudinal), and why or how (qual) vs how many (quant).

sources.name: Steve Krug: Don't Make Me Think, Revisited (3rd ed.), Rocket Surgery Made Easy, and downloadable test kit
sources.version_or_date: Don't Make Me Think Revisited 2014 (3rd ed.); Rocket Surgery Made Easy 2010; test scripts dated © 2013
sources.license: copyright Steve Krug. The downloads may be shared with individuals with the copyright notice intact, but must not be reposted online, so link to the page instead. The books are all rights reserved.
sources.license_evidence: https://sensible.com/download-files/ (FAQ on the page); script PDF header at https://www.stevekrug.com/downloads/test-script-desktop.pdf
sources.summary: The do-it-yourself usability testing playbook. The free kit includes facilitator scripts for web, mobile and desktop tests, a recording-consent form, a prep checklist timed weeks ahead, a list of neutral facilitator phrases, and an observer handout. On that handout, each observer records the top three problems seen per session for a lunch debrief. The script stresses that the product is being tested, not the participant, asks for think-aloud, and has the facilitator deflect questions to see how people cope without help.

key_items.name: Standard facilitator script
key_items.one_line: Read a fixed intro covering purpose, 'we test the product, not you', think-aloud and recording consent, so every session starts the same way.
key_items.use_when: Running or generating a moderated test session.

key_items.name: Observer top-3 + debrief
key_items.one_line: Each observer notes the three worst problems per session, and the team agrees on fixes in a short debrief.
key_items.use_when: Turning sessions into a fix list fast.

key_items.name: Small, frequent rounds
key_items.one_line: Rocket Surgery's cadence is a few users in a recurring short session with fixes chosen right after. The exact 'three users, a morning a month' wording was NOT verified against the primary text here.
key_items.use_when: Building a lightweight recurring test habit.

key_items.name: Self-evident design
key_items.one_line: Don't Make Me Think's core heuristic: pages should be self-evident, or at least self-explanatory, so users don't have to stop and puzzle things out.
key_items.use_when: Quick critique of a screen before testing.

sources.name: System Usability Scale (Brooke) with MeasuringU benchmarks and interpretation (Sauro)
sources.publisher: MeasuringU (Jeff Sauro); instrument by John Brooke, Digital Equipment Corp.
sources.version_or_date: SUS created 1986 per MeasuringU (usually cited from its 1996 book-chapter publication); benchmark of about 500 studies; MeasuringU 2025 business-software benchmark still uses 68
sources.license: Page content: copyright MeasuringU, all rights reserved (© footer; no open license found). The SUS instrument itself is widely described as free to use, but that was not verified here.
sources.summary: A 10-item, 5-point questionnaire with alternating positive and negative items. Scoring: odd items contribute (response-1), even items (5-response), and the sum is multiplied by 2.5 for a 0-100 range. The average across about 500 studies is 68, which sits at the 50th percentile. A score is not a percentage, so convert it to a percentile or grade (above about 80.3 is roughly the top 10%). SUS is reliable even at small n but imprecise, so report confidence intervals. It is not diagnostic, and it correlates only modestly with task performance (r ≈ .24).

key_items.name: Scoring rule
key_items.one_line: Odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum ×2.5, giving a 0-100 scale.

key_items.name: 68 = average (50th percentile)
key_items.one_line: Above 68 is above average. Report percentile ranks or grades, not 'X% usable'.
key_items.use_when: Explaining a SUS result to stakeholders.

key_items.name: Usability + learnability
key_items.one_line: Items 4 and 10 form a learnability subscale, and the other 8 items cover usability.

key_items.name: Not diagnostic
key_items.one_line: A low SUS says that something is wrong, not what. Pair it with observed sessions.
key_items.use_when: Someone wants to fix design from SUS alone.

key_items.name: Report confidence intervals
key_items.one_line: Small samples give unstable means, so always show the interval around the mean.

sources.name: Single Ease Question (Sauro & Dumas, CHI 2009) and MeasuringU SEQ norms
sources.publisher: MeasuringU; original comparison published by ACM (CHI 2009)
sources.version_or_date: Sauro & Dumas CHI 2009; MeasuringU 'Evolution of the SEQ' 2024 (adjective labels added 2023)
sources.license: MeasuringU page: copyright MeasuringU (© footer). CHI paper: Copyright 2009 ACM.
sources.license_evidence: https://measuringu.com/papers/Sauro_Dumas_CHI2009.pdf (ACM copyright line in PDF); https://measuringu.com/evolution-of-seq/ (© footer)
sources.summary: A single 7-point 'how easy or difficult was this task' rating asked right after each task. Sauro & Dumas found it performed about as well as more elaborate one-question measures (SMEQ, magnitude estimation). MeasuringU's norms put the average near 5.5: early data suggested about 5, and a score around 5.5 is the 50th percentile. An average SEQ corresponds to roughly a 71% task completion rate.

key_items.name: One post-task item
key_items.one_line: Ask ease on a 7-point scale right after each task, alongside observed success and time.
key_items.use_when: Every task in a usability test or benchmark.

key_items.name: Average ≈ 5.5
key_items.one_line: Below about 5.5 means harder than a typical task, so flag it for qualitative review.

key_items.name: Ease vs success
key_items.one_line: Perceived ease and actual completion are related but separate. Users can fail a task and still rate it easy, so report both.

sources.name: UMUX-LITE: when there's no time for the SUS (Lewis, Utesch & Maher, CHI 2013) and MeasuringU UX-Lite
sources.version_or_date: UMUX-LITE 2013; UX-Lite (5-point adaptation) introduced by MeasuringU, article dated 2021
sources.license: Copyright © 2013 ACM (paper). MeasuringU UX-Lite page: copyright MeasuringU.
sources.license_evidence: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2470654.2481287 (ACM copyright line read from the paper PDF); https://measuringu.com/evolution-of-the-ux-lite/
sources.summary: A two-item perceived-usability measure: one item on whether the system's capabilities meet the user's requirements (usefulness) and one on ease of use. Reliability was about .82-.83, and it correlated about .81 with SUS. Raw means run slightly below SUS, and a published linear regression maps them onto the SUS scale. It suits in-product intercepts where 10 items is too many. MeasuringU's UX-Lite is a 5-point adaptation.

key_items.name: Two items: useful + usable
key_items.one_line: Covers functional adequacy and ease of use in two questions.
key_items.use_when: In-app surveys and post-release pulse checks.

key_items.name: Regress to SUS scale
key_items.one_line: Apply the published regression before comparing with SUS benchmarks such as 68.
key_items.use_when: Comparing UMUX-LITE results with SUS norms.

sources.name: Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications (Google HEART; Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, CHI 2010)
sources.license: © ACM 2010. The author's version is posted by permission of ACM for personal use and is not for redistribution.
sources.summary: HEART stands for Happiness (attitudinal: satisfaction, perceived ease, likelihood to recommend), Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success (effectiveness and efficiency). The categories prompt user-centered metric choice and complement business or technical metrics such as Google's PULSE set (page views, uptime, latency, seven-day actives, earnings). Teams need not use every category, but should decide explicitly what to include, at product or feature level. The Goals-Signals-Metrics process goes from agreed goals, to the behavioral or attitudinal signals that would show success (from logs or surveys), to specific trackable metrics.

key_items.name: Happiness
key_items.one_line: Attitudinal metrics from regular, well-designed surveys, tracked over time.
key_items.use_when: Satisfaction or perception is the goal.

key_items.name: Engagement
key_items.one_line: Frequency, intensity or depth of use per user over a period. It may not make sense for mandatory enterprise tools.

key_items.name: Adoption
key_items.one_line: New users of the product or a feature in a period.

key_items.name: Retention
key_items.one_line: Share of users from one period who are still active in a later one.

key_items.name: Task success
key_items.one_line: Efficiency, effectiveness and error rate, from logs or tests.
key_items.use_when: Task-oriented flows such as search, checkout or forms.

key_items.name: Goals → Signals → Metrics
key_items.one_line: Agree goals first, then pick the signals that would move, then define metrics. Don't start from whatever is already logged.
key_items.use_when: Any time a dashboard or success metric is being defined.

key_items.name: Explicitly pick categories
key_items.one_line: Use HEART as a checklist for including or excluding each category, not a mandate to track all five.

sources.name: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing (Kohavi, Tang & Xu) with ExP papers on SRM and unexpected results
sources.publisher: Cambridge University Press (book); Microsoft ExP / ACM KDD (papers)
sources.version_or_date: Book 2020; Fabijan et al. SRM taxonomy KDD 2019; Kohavi et al. 'Unexpected Results' SIGKDD Explorations 2010
sources.license: Book: copyright (c)2020 Kohavi, Tang & Xu, published by Cambridge University Press (chapter 1 is a free sample PDF). KDD 2019 paper: copyright held by the owner/authors with ACM publication rights.
sources.summary: The reference for running A/B tests whose results can be trusted. Agree one Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) up front that predicts long-term value, since revenue or profit alone is a poor OEC. Treat surprising results with suspicion (Twyman's law: a truly unexpected result is probably wrong) and check data quality first. Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) is a key trust check, and about 6% of Microsoft experiments showed one. Expect most ideas to fail: about one third of ideas tested at Microsoft improved their target metric, and in well-optimized domains like Bing and Google success rates are about 10-20%.

key_items.name: Overall Evaluation Criterion
key_items.one_line: Pre-register one composite success metric aligned with long-term value before launch.

key_items.name: Sample Ratio Mismatch check
key_items.one_line: If the observed traffic split differs significantly from the designed split, do not trust the results until the cause is found.
key_items.use_when: First step of every experiment readout.

key_items.name: Twyman's law
key_items.one_line: Unusually large or surprising effects most often come from bugs or instrumentation. Investigate before celebrating.

key_items.name: Most ideas fail
key_items.one_line: About a third of Microsoft ideas helped, and 10-20% in mature domains, so humility and testing beat intuition.
key_items.use_when: Arguing for testing rather than shipping on opinion.

sources.name: Continuous Discovery Habits / Product Talk (Teresa Torres)
sources.publisher: Product Talk LLC (book: Continuous Discovery Habits, 2021)
sources.version_or_date: Book 2021; Product Talk articles accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: copyright Product Talk / Teresa Torres (© 2026 footer; no open license found)
sources.summary: Discovery is an ongoing habit, not a phase. The team that builds the product engages customers at least weekly so fewer decisions are made without customer input. The opportunity solution tree puts a desired outcome at the root, customer opportunities (needs and pain points) found in interviews below it, then candidate solutions, then small assumption tests. Torres teaches story-based interviews that collect specific past behavior rather than opinions or wish lists.

key_items.name: Weekly customer touchpoints
key_items.one_line: Keep a recurring cadence of small research activities aimed at a specific outcome.

key_items.name: Opportunity solution tree
key_items.one_line: Outcome → opportunities → solutions → assumption tests, which makes the link from evidence to decision visible.

key_items.name: Story-based interviewing
key_items.one_line: Ask about a specific recent instance ('tell me about the last time...') instead of hypotheticals.

key_items.name: Test assumptions, not whole ideas
key_items.one_line: Break solutions into the riskiest assumptions and test those cheaply first.
key_items.use_when: Before committing to building a solution.

sources.name: Jobs to Be Done theory (Christensen Institute; Christensen et al., HBR 2016) with Moesta/Spiek forces of progress
sources.publisher: Clayton Christensen Institute; Harvard Business Review; forces model via jobstobedone.org (secondary)
sources.version_or_date: HBR 'Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done' Sept 2016; Competing Against Luck 2016; institute page accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: Christensen Institute: © 2016-2026 Clayton Christensen Institute, all rights reserved. HBR: copyright, paywalled. jobstobedone.org: unknown.
sources.summary: People do not just buy products. They pull them into their lives to make progress in a particular circumstance, and that progress (functional, social and emotional) is the job. Understanding the circumstance explains choice better than demographics or product attributes. Moesta and Spiek's switch-interview model (reported via jobstobedone.org) says a switch happens only when the push of the current situation plus the pull of the new solution outweigh anxiety about the new and habit of the present.

key_items.name: Job = progress in a circumstance
key_items.one_line: Frame needs as 'when [situation], I want to [progress], so I can [outcome]', not as features.

key_items.name: Four forces of progress
key_items.one_line: Push + pull must beat anxiety + habit. Design to reduce anxiety and habit, not only to add pull.
key_items.use_when: Diagnosing low adoption or failed switching.

key_items.name: Switch interview timeline
key_items.one_line: Rebuild the real purchase or switch timeline from first thought to use, to see which forces acted.

sources.name: Outcome-Driven Innovation (Tony Ulwick / Strategyn)
sources.version_or_date: ODI since 1990s; Jobs to be Done: Theory to Practice (2016); page accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: Copyright Strategyn, all rights reserved. Outcome-Driven Innovation® is a registered trademark.
sources.summary: A quantitative JTBD method. Map the customer's job, write desired-outcome statements (customer-defined success metrics for each job step), survey importance and satisfaction for each, and rank them by opportunity = importance + max(0, importance - satisfaction). Underserved outcomes, high in importance and low in satisfaction, are the targets.

key_items.name: Desired-outcome statements
key_items.one_line: Write each need as a measurable outcome the customer wants to improve, with no solution words.
key_items.use_when: Turning interview notes into a needs inventory.

key_items.name: Opportunity score
key_items.one_line: Opportunity = importance + max(0, importance - satisfaction). Over-served outcomes are not penalized below importance.

sources.name: GOV.UK Service Manual: User research and Measuring success
sources.version_or_date: Living guidance, accessed 2026-10-15
sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0 (except where otherwise stated), © Crown copyright
sources.license_evidence: https://www.gov.uk/help/terms-conditions (and the site footer: 'All content is available under the Open Government Licence v3.0')
sources.summary: An openly licensed, phase-based research handbook covering user research in discovery, alpha, beta and live; planning rounds; recruitment briefs; informed consent; research with disabled people; data and privacy handling; and methods (contextual research, interviews, moderated usability testing, pop-up and remote research, analysis). Its moderated-testing guide gives concrete logistics: 30-60 minute sessions, no more than 6 a day with at least 15-minute gaps, a note-taker per session, and tasks with clear, believable goals that do not give away the answer. The Measuring success section covers performance metrics, benchmarking, and the standard service measures: digital take-up, user satisfaction, completion rate and cost per transaction. Under OGL, the plugin can adapt this text with attribution, not just link to it.

key_items.name: Research by phase
key_items.one_line: Each phase (discovery, alpha, beta, live) has its own research goals and methods.
key_items.use_when: Picking research for where the project is in its lifecycle.

key_items.name: Moderated usability testing logistics
key_items.one_line: Session length, daily cap, gaps, observers and note-taker, and recording decisions are all planned up front.

key_items.name: Task design rules
key_items.one_line: Tasks should have a clear goal, be realistic for participants, be hard enough to expose issues, and not hint at the solution.

key_items.name: Informed consent and data handling
key_items.one_line: Get informed consent and manage participant data and privacy as first-class steps.

key_items.name: Standard service KPIs
key_items.one_line: Measure digital take-up, user satisfaction, completion rate and cost per transaction, then add service-specific metrics.
key_items.use_when: Defining success metrics for a transactional service.

sources.name: 18F Methods (human-centered design method cards)
sources.version_or_date: Repository archived (read-only) May 31, 2024
sources.license: Public domain in the US; CC0 1.0 Universal dedication worldwide
sources.summary: A public-domain deck of human-centered design method cards that 18F used across research, synthesis, prototyping and validation, each with when to use it, time required and steps. Because it is CC0, the plugin can copy and adapt method cards verbatim into its own skills. The repository is archived and frozen, so treat it as stable but unmaintained.

key_items.name: Copyable method cards
key_items.one_line: CC0 means card text can be embedded directly in skills without attribution constraints, though citing it is still good practice.

sources.summary: Operational scaffolding so research stays consistent and reusable. The ResearchOps Community model has eight pillars: environment, scope, people, organisational context, recruitment and admin, data and knowledge management, governance, and tools and infrastructure. NN/g's model treats ResearchOps as a part of DesignOps with six components: participant management, governance, knowledge management, tools, competency and advocacy.
