claims.claim: Nielsen & Landauer (1993) modeled usability-problem discovery across 11 studies (user tests and heuristic evaluation) as a Poisson process with mean single-user/evaluator detection probability about .31.
claims.note: jev verified. It flagged numbers_missing ['1993','31'], but these are tokenization artifacts: grep confirms the PDF text has 'N=41, and λ=.31' (OCR renders λ as 'b'). Checked against the PDF text as indexed by Perplexity, because ACM DL blocked direct fetch.

claims.claim: NN/g: discovering all usability problems needs at least about 15 users; 5-user rounds are recommended because iterative rounds are more valuable.
claims.note: Split claim c02a. The original compound claim (15 users AND 'only holds for one user group') came back contradicted at 0.61 because of the wording, so it was split into two parts and both were verified.

claims.claim: The five-user formula only holds for comparable users using the product in similar ways; distinct user groups need their own participants (3-4 per group for two groups, 3 per group for three or more).
claims.note: Split claim c02b.

claims.claim: In Faulkner (2003), with 60 users tested, random sets of five participants found between about 55% and 99% of the problems.
claims.note: Checked against the Springer abstract text (primary) and also against MeasuringU's history page (secondary). Both verified.

claims.claim: Spool & Schroeder (2001) found four production websites would need considerably more than five users to find 85% of problems.
claims.note: Checked against ACM abstract text indexed by Perplexity. Jev's numbers_missing ['2001'] refers only to the year.

claims.claim: In Nielsen's Guerrilla HCI case study the best-fit detection rate was λ = 0.26, not 0.31.
claims.note: Shows λ is project-specific.

claims.claim: COMMON MISQUOTE: 'Testing any product with five users always finds 85% of its usability problems.'
claims.note: Primary text: individual 5-user samples found 55%-99%. 85% is an average that assumes λ≈.31 and one homogeneous user group, and NN/g itself says about 15 users are needed for full coverage.

claims.claim: Nielsen's severity scale runs 0-4 (4 = usability catastrophe); severity combines frequency, impact, persistence (plus market impact); single-evaluator severity is unreliable, so use the mean of about three evaluators.
claims.note: Jev review=true (0.74) because this is a compound claim. Each part matches the page text on manual read.

claims.claim: In heuristic evaluation, single evaluators found only about 35% of usability problems on average (over six projects); Nielsen recommends three to five evaluators.
claims.note: Deliberately NOT claimed: any '5 evaluators find 75%' figure. It was not found in the fetched primary text.

claims.claim: COMMON MISQUOTE: 'An expert heuristic evaluation can replace usability testing with real users.'
claims.note: NN/g states that heuristic evaluations cannot replace user research. They complement it.

claims.claim: The average SUS score across about 500 studies is 68, the 50th percentile; SUS scores are not percentages.
COMMON MISQUOTE: 'A SUS score of 68 means 68% usability / the 68th percentile.'
claims.note: Primary text: 68 is the average, at the 50th percentile, and SUS scores are explicitly not percentages.

claims.claim: SUS correlates only modestly with task performance (around r = .24) and is not diagnostic of specific problems.
claims.note: Jev's numbers_missing ['24'] is an artifact: the source text reads 'r=.24'.

claims.claim: SUS was created by John Brooke in 1986 as a 'quick and dirty' scale administered after usability tests.
claims.note: Version note: the usual academic citation is Brooke's 1996 book chapter. That 1996 date was not checked here.

claims.claim: The average Single Ease Question score is about 5.5 on its 7-point scale (earlier benchmarks suggested about 5).
claims.note: Vendor blogs (koji.so, uxtweak) quote 5.3-5.6. They were dropped by jev rank in favor of the MeasuringU primary.

claims.claim: UMUX-LITE has two items (capabilities meet requirements; easy to use) and correlates with SUS at about .81, with a regression adjustment to the SUS scale.
claims.note: Jev's numbers_missing ['81'] is an artifact: the source text reads '(.81, .81)'. The text came from an author PDF mirror (iihm.imag.fr) because ACM DL was blocked.

claims.claim: HEART = Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success; teams need not use metrics from every category.
COMMON MISQUOTE: 'The HEART framework requires tracking metrics in all five categories.'
claims.note: The paper says it is not always appropriate to use every category, and that the framework is for deciding explicitly what to include.

claims.claim: The HEART paper's process steps teams from goals, to signals, to specific metrics (Goals-Signals-Metrics).
Only about one third of ideas tested at Microsoft improved the metrics they were designed to improve; in well-optimized domains like Bing and Google the success rate is about 10-20%.
claims.note: Checked against the free Chapter 1 PDF of the 2020 book. The book cites Kohavi, Crook & Longbotham 2009 and Manzi 2012.

claims.claim: About 6% of online controlled experiments at Microsoft exhibited a sample ratio mismatch.
NN/g recommends 40 participants for most quantitative usability studies, sized for about a 15% margin of error at 95% confidence.
claims.note: Jev review=true (0.79). The page text states both the number 40 and the 15% / 95% basis.

claims.claim: COMMON MISQUOTE: 'NN/g currently recommends 20 participants for quantitative usability studies.'
claims.note: 20 was the 2006 recommendation (quantitative-studies-how-many-users). NN/g now recommends 40 and acknowledges it has changed the number over the years.

claims.claim: ODI opportunity score = importance + max(0, importance - satisfaction).
COMMON MISQUOTE: 'In ODI the opportunity score is simply importance minus satisfaction.'
claims.note: Third-party summaries such as andrewclark.co.uk state it this way. The primary formula adds importance and clamps the gap at zero.

claims.claim: Teresa Torres: good product discovery teams engage with customers at least weekly.
Krug's Rocket Surgery cadence is 'three users, one morning a month' with a lunch debrief.
claims.note: This wording was seen only in a third-party GitHub skill file. The primary downloads page and script do not state it, and the book was not accessible. Mark it unverified.

claims.claim: Cognitive walkthrough asks four questions at each step (try to achieve the right result; notice the correct action; associate action with goal; see progress after acting), and a step fails if any answer is no.
claims.note: Confirmed by grep of the NN/g page text (all four questions and the fail rule are present), but no jev call was run. The original 1994 practitioner's guide PDF is a scan with no extractable text.

claims.claim: ISO 9241-11:2018 defines usability as the extent to which specified users achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
claims.note: The ISO page was blocked by bot protection. The definition is widely cited but was not verified here.

claims.claim: NN/g's 10 usability heuristics date from 1994 and have remained unchanged; the article was updated with more explanation in 2020.
claims.note: Seen in page text by grep. No jev call was run.

mapping_ideas: new-playbook:usability-test-round - The agent writes the research questions, recruit spec (about 5 per distinct user group, 3-4 per group if there are two groups), realistic tasks that don't give away the answer, a facilitator script, a consent form and an observer sheet. A human runs the sessions. The agent then synthesizes top problems with severity and a fix list, and schedules the next 5-user round to re-test the fixes. Grounded in Krug's kit, the NN/g 5-user article, Nielsen & Landauer 1993, and GOV.UK moderated usability testing (OGL, adaptable).

new-playbook:heuristic-review - The agent runs several separate review passes (different heuristic lenses or sub-agents, with no sharing until consolidation), consolidates findings, rates each 0-4 using frequency, impact and persistence, and averages severities. It labels every finding as a HYPOTHESIS to validate with users. It does NOT claim the Nielsen-Landauer coverage percentage, because model-generated passes are not statistically independent evaluators. Grounded in the NN/g how-to, theory and severity articles.

new-playbook:cognitive-walkthrough - For each step of the correct path, the agent answers the four learnability questions, marks a step failed if any answer is no, and outputs a pass/fail trace per task that can be used directly as an evidence log. Grounded in the NN/g cognitive-walkthroughs article (Wharton et al. 1994).

new-playbook:ux-metrics-plan - The agent writes Goals, then Signals, then Metrics per HEART category. It decides explicitly which categories to include or exclude, at product or feature level, and pairs the plan with GOV.UK's standard service KPIs where relevant. Grounded in Rodden et al. 2010 and GOV.UK Measuring success.

new-playbook:ux-benchmark-study - The agent sizes the sample (about 40 for roughly ±15% at 95%) and picks instruments (SEQ after each task, SUS or UMUX-LITE at the end, task success and time-on-task). It computes confidence intervals and reports percentiles against norms (SUS 68 = 50th percentile, SEQ about 5.5), never 'SUS 70 = 70%'. Grounded in the NN/g quant summary, MeasuringU SUS and SEQ, and Lewis et al. 2013.

new-playbook:experiment-readout - Before reading the result, the agent checks that an OEC was pre-registered, runs the SRM test, applies Twyman's law to surprising effects, checks guardrails, and states the base rate that most ideas fail. Grounded in Kohavi, Tang & Xu 2020 and Fabijan et al. 2019.

new-playbook:discovery-interview-cycle - The agent keeps a weekly cadence, writes story-based interview guides about a specific last time, keeps per-interview snapshots, and maintains an opportunity solution tree with assumption tests for each candidate solution. Grounded in Torres's Continuous Discovery Habits and Product Talk.

new-playbook:jtbd-switch-interview - The agent rebuilds the switch timeline for recent adopters and churners and codes the push, pull, anxiety and habit forces. Design work targets reducing anxiety and habit, not only adding pull. Grounded in the Christensen Institute JTBD theory and the Moesta/Spiek forces model.

new-playbook:jtbd-outcome-survey - The agent maps job steps and writes solution-free desired-outcome statements. It scores opportunity = importance + max(0, importance - satisfaction), using the correct formula, and ranks underserved outcomes. Grounded in Strategyn ODI.

new-playbook:research-plan - The agent picks methods by question type (behavioral vs attitudinal, qualitative vs quantitative) and by lifecycle phase (discovery, alpha, beta, live), and plans consent and data handling up front. Grounded in GOV.UK user research, NN/g which-ux-research-methods, and 18F Methods (CC0, adaptable).

new-playbook:research-repository - The agent files every study's findings with linked evidence, consent status and retention date, so insights are reusable and audit-ready. Grounded in the ResearchOps Community pillars and NN/g ResearchOps 101.

principle:prove-it-works -> design-stack 'validate-with-users-not-reviewers' - Inspection, AI critique and stakeholder opinion produce hypotheses. Only observed user behavior, or a trustworthy experiment, counts as proof. Grounded in NN/g ('heuristic evaluations cannot replace user research') and Kohavi's base rates.

principle:explain-the-number -> 'compare-to-a-benchmark' - Never report a UX metric alone. Give the comparison (previous version, competitor, or norm such as SUS 68 or SEQ 5.5), the confidence interval and the sample size. Grounded in the NN/g quant articles and MeasuringU.

new-principle:size-the-sample-to-the-question - Qualitative rounds use about 5 per homogeneous group and iterate. Quantitative studies use about 40. Card sorts use about 15 per group. Never quote '5 users find 85%' without λ, the homogeneity caveat and the 55-99% variance. Grounded in Nielsen & Landauer, NN/g, Faulkner 2003, and Spool & Schroeder 2001.

new-principle:severity-not-count - Prioritize by mean severity (0-4) from several raters, not by the raw number of findings. Release gates key on any open 4 (catastrophe). Grounded in NN/g severity ratings.

new-principle:triangulate-before-concluding - A finding becomes a decision input only when a second method or source agrees, for example think-aloud plus analytics, or SUS plus observed task failure, since SUS is not diagnostic. Grounded in NN/g triangulation and MeasuringU on SUS and task-performance correlation.

principle:never-block-on-the-human -> 'prepare-the-study-not-the-verdict' - When real participants are needed, the agent never stalls and never fakes results. It produces a ready-to-run study kit (plan, tasks, script, consent, instruments, analysis template), runs proxy methods (heuristic review, cognitive walkthrough) meanwhile, and labels proxy output as unvalidated. Grounded in Krug's kit, GOV.UK and NN/g.

principle:test-behavior-not-implementation -> 'observe-behavior-over-opinion' - Base design conclusions on what users did on realistic tasks (think-aloud, task success), not on what they say they would do. Grounded in NN/g think-aloud, Torres story-based interviewing, and the JTBD switch interview.

INSTALL/REFERENCE RECOMMENDATION. The strongest replacements for pstack's code-centric verification are split by how their content can be used:
(a) Adaptable, open-licensed text that can live inside skills: GOV.UK Service Manual (OGL v3, needs attribution) and 18F Methods (CC0, archived May 31, 2024).
(b) Cite-and-link only, all rights reserved: NN/g (links and short quotes are explicitly allowed), MeasuringU, the HEART author PDF (ACM: not for redistribution), Kohavi (Cambridge UP; chapter 1 is a free PDF), Torres, Christensen Institute, Strategyn (ODI is a registered trademark), and Krug. Krug's downloads may be shared with the copyright notice intact but must not be reposted, so the plugin should link to sensible.com/download-files.
Licenses still unknown: Faulkner (Springer) and Spool & Schroeder (ACM), because their license pages were not fetchable; the ResearchOps Community; jobstobedone.org.

VERSION NOTES as of 2026-10-15:
- NN/g's quantitative sample size moved from 20 (2006) to 40 (current summary article).
- UX-Lite (MeasuringU, 5-point) adapts UMUX-LITE (2013).
- SEQ norms moved from about 5 to about 5.5. Adjective labels were added in 2023.
- NN/g's 10 heuristics are unchanged since 1994. The article was expanded in 2020.
- SUS: MeasuringU dates its creation to 1986. The 1996 chapter citation was not checked.
- Kohavi's book is from 2020, Continuous Discovery Habits from 2021, Don't Make Me Think Revisited from 2014, and Rocket Surgery Made Easy from 2010 (scripts © 2013).
- ISO 9241-11:2018 could not be verified because the page was blocked.
- 18F Methods' archival status is verified from GitHub. The broader status of the 18F organization was not checked.

COMMONLY MISQUOTED NUMBERS, each checked with jev against its primary source (all came back contradicted):
1. '5 users find 85% of problems' is an average that assumes λ≈.31 and a single homogeneous user group. Individual samples ranged 55-99% (Faulkner). Complex websites needed far more users (Spool & Schroeder). λ was .26 in Guerrilla HCI. NN/g itself says about 15 users are needed for full coverage.
2. 'SUS 68 = 68%': it is the 50th percentile, and SUS scores are not percentages.
3. 'NN/g says 20 for quant': that is outdated, and the current figure is 40.
4. 'ODI opportunity = importance - satisfaction': the gap is clamped at zero and added to importance.
5. 'HEART means track all five': the paper says choose explicitly.
6. 'Expert review can replace testing': NN/g says no.
Also avoided: any '5 evaluators find 75%' figure, which was not in the fetched primary text. The supported figure is that a single evaluator finds about 35%, and Nielsen recommends 3-5 evaluators.

JEV: 29 checks ran (c01-c20 plus the split c02a/c02b, m01-m06, and Guerrilla λ). The compound c02 came back contradicted at 0.61 because of its wording. It was split, and both halves were verified, so it is reported here rather than hidden. numbers_missing flags on c01 (31), c12 (81) and c20 (24) are decimal-tokenization artifacts; grep confirmed '.31', '.81' and 'r=.24' are in the sources. jev rank ordered 16 candidates: HEART, NN/g quant-40, NN/g 5-user, severity, SUS and heuristic evaluation scored 0.84-0.90, and GOV.UK 0.81. Vendor blogs (koji.so, uxtweak) scored 0.53-0.57 and were dropped. Torres and Strategyn ranked low (0.26-0.29) for a 'metrics with numbers' query but were kept, because they cover the discovery/JTBD sub-angle.

DESIGN CAVEAT for the plugin: never-block-on-the-human conflicts with methods that need real participants. The resolution proposed in mapping_ideas is to prepare the full study kit, run proxy inspections meanwhile, and label proxy output as unvalidated hypotheses. Also, parallel model 'evaluators' are not independent in the Nielsen-Landauer sense, so keep independent passes and averaged severity, but do not claim coverage percentages.

Primary text files (for re-checking) are under <local-scratch> and jev outputs are under .../scratchpad/ux/jev/.

Phase coverage is lopsided. The agent handbooks cluster around UI craft, design QA and accessibility. Discovery/define and measure are thin. sources.summary: Delegate. A single skill that works like a router: its argument picks a sub-command playbook (shape, critique, audit, polish, harden, typeset, layout, colorize, animate, onboard, optimize, adapt, distill, clarify, init/document/extract/live). A launcher loads PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md context. The skill reads a 'craft floor' reference before any UI edit and limits self-verification to bounded passes. Its critique scores Nielsen's 10 heuristics 0-4, renormalizes explicitly when a heuristic is n/a, and saves snapshots so later runs can show a trend. Of everything here, it is the closest structural sibling to poteto-mode for UI craft. It has no discovery, research or measurement commands (confirmed by the Codex second read).

sources.summary: Delegate through the web-design-guidelines skill, and adapt the text where useful (MIT), for code-level UI rules. It is a living, framework-agnostic list of interface decisions in eight sections: Interactions, Animations, Layout, Content, Forms, Performance, Design and Copywriting. It ships in three forms: the README, a drop-in AGENTS.md for code generation, and command.md as a terse review prompt. The rules are concrete and checkable: keyboard operability per WAI-ARIA APG, visible focus, hit targets of at least 24px (44px on mobile), reduced-motion support, no transition:all, URL as state, confirmation or undo for destructive actions. Several link to WCAG 2.2 Understanding pages.

sources.summary: Adapt (MIT): copy the workflow with attribution and upgrade its accessibility standard. The package is a Claude Code subagent, a /design-review slash command, a CLAUDE.md snippet and an example design-principles document. Together they review front-end diffs in a live Playwright session in seven phases: interaction flow; responsiveness at 1440, 768 and 375px; visual polish; accessibility; robustness (invalid input, overflow, loading/empty/error states); code health (token use, component reuse); and content plus console. playbook:visual-parity (upgrade): add dyl-stack's gates (intake blocks coding, map to repo primitives and tokens only, visual judge VERIFIED) and delegate Figma mechanics to figma-design-to-code.

new-playbook:design-system-build: tokens in DTCG 2025.10 format (state the version in $schema), components mapped through Code Connect, and a library generated or synced in Figma. Delegates to Figma generate-library/code-connect and plugin87 tokens/gates; grounded in the DTCG spec.
new-playbook:design-handoff: produce a spec with tokens, states, breakpoints, motion and edge cases. Delegates to Figma figma-spec and the Anthropic design-handoff template.

new-playbook:measure-outcomes: define one metric that matters per release, attach CWV/Lighthouse numbers and task-success metrics, and compare against the hypothesis from define-problem. new-principle:cite-the-current-standard: every rule an agent applies names its standard, version and criterion ID, and the agent flags stale versions it encounters (WCAG 2.1 to 2.2, unversioned DTCG to 2025.10). Grounded in this research's own findings on the Anthropic design plugin and OneRedOak.
new-principle:fetch-rules-fresh: fetch fast-moving rulebooks at run time instead of vendoring them. Grounded in Vercel's web-design-guidelines skill.
new-principle:live-environment-first: judge the running, interactive UI before reading static code or screenshots. Grounded in OneRedOak design-review; pairs with principle:experience-first.
new-principle:problems-over-prescriptions: review comments state the user impact and the violated heuristic or criterion, not a CSS fix. Grounded in OneRedOak.

new-principle:delegate-do-not-copy: when a maintained, licensed skill exists, point at it and verify its output instead of restating it; never copy unlicensed text (Figma). Grounded in dyl-stack build-figma.
new-principle:worst-case-content: test every screen with long, empty, huge and malformed content before calling it done. Grounded in emil break-ui and OneRedOak Phase 5.

principle:never-block-on-the-human (design variant): when no user research exists, proceed on stated, labeled assumptions and schedule a validation step instead of stalling. Grounded in Owl start-here sequencing and wondelai lean-ux hypotheses.

mapping_ideas: new-playbook:ux-review-router (/design-mode core) - route a design task to category leaf skills (forms, a11y, navigation, errors, visual, IA, copy) with one shared findings format, as poteto-mode does for engineering - grounded in parhamb/design-skills ux-review router + poteto-mode.

new-principle:design-plan-before-pixels - write a token plan (4-6 named colors, type roles, ASCII layout, principles), compare it with the generic default, revise and say why, then code - grounded in anthropics frontend-design SKILL.md.

new-principle:ground-in-the-subject - identify subject, audience and primary job before visual choices; when missing, state an assumption and keep going rather than blocking - grounded in frontend-design (which says to confirm with the client) + principle:never-block-on-the-human.

new-principle:name-the-heuristic - every design decision cites the heuristic, law or rule ID that changed it (Nielsen #n, Laws of UX law, WIG rule, WCAG 2.2 SC), the design version of poteto's name-the-principle rule - grounded in @poteto 2110496830429839869 + ux-heuristics.

new-playbook:design-critique-loop - build, screenshot at 375/768/1280, critique with impeccable critique or the Nielsen scorecard, fix, re-screenshot, and attach before/after evidence - grounded in @0xrux loop, Impeccable, frontend-design self-critique.

new-playbook:design-qa (independent visual-bug hunter) - a second agent that sees only the rendered UI hunts clipped text, invisible focus, broken mobile tables and invisible primary actions; then run worst-case content - grounded in @educalvolpz 2110038211678355706, @aryanXmahajan, emilkowalski break-ui.
new-principle:worst-case-content - render every data-bearing component with long, empty, huge, non-Latin and emoji content before calling it done - grounded in emilkowalski/skills break-ui.

new-principle:detector-is-evidence-not-proof (design prove-it-works) - a passing lint, detector or WIG review is necessary but not sufficient; inspect the rendered experience at the target viewports - grounded in Impeccable README + HIGAgentSkills enforce mode.

new-playbook:token-drift-audit - crawl the running app, list off-system color/spacing/type values, trace each to a missing token or unwritten decision, then encode it in DESIGN.md or tokens - grounded in @JeffWitters + Impeccable designSystem detector mode + awesome-design-md format.

new-principle:avoid-distributional-defaults - name the default look the model would produce and choose against it unless the brief asks for it; refresh the tell-list regularly because defaults drift - grounded in the Anthropic skills article + frontend-design calibration list + @tiennguyendev.
new-principle:tokens-before-brief - load the product's tokens/DESIGN.md before describing any screen - grounded in @tiennguyendev + awesome-design-md DESIGN.md format.

new-playbook:evidence-pack-handoff - instead of asking taste questions, ship screenshots and a staging link to a human-review column and keep working; taste and QC sign-off stay human - grounded in @tangentstorm, @aryanXmahajan; reconciles principle:never-block-on-the-human with designers keeping taste.

angles.notes:
The community converges on four installs: Impeccable, Anthropic frontend-design, Taste Skill and Vercel's Web Interface Guidelines (wrapped by vercel-labs web-design-guidelines). ui-ux-pro-max-skill (MIT, ~136k stars, a searchable catalog of palettes, font pairings and styles) is also popular but is a data catalog rather than a method, so it was left out of sources. Classic handbooks (Nielsen's 10, Laws of UX, Gestalt, Refactoring UI, Apple HIG, WCAG 2.2) reach agents only through distilled skills, never as the handbook itself. The design-stack should do the same and cite the primary handbook in each leaf.

pstack signal: there is heavy praise and many ports. michael-denyer/pstack-claude (MIT, ~2.1k stars) ports poteto-mode and the principle skills to Claude Code, a useful reference for the router mechanics. sources.name: Deceptive Patterns: Types of deceptive pattern (formerly darkpatterns.org)
sources.license: All rights reserved (copyright 2026 Testimonium Ltd; terms say the service and its original content are the company's exclusive property). Link and paraphrase only. Never vendor.
sources.version_or_date: Live taxonomy read 2026-10-15. 18 types listed by my own count; the site keeps adding types (Addictive Design and Currency Confusion have examples but no laws mapped yet).
sources.summary: The standard catalogue of manipulative UI patterns. Every type has a one-line definition and is linked to the laws, rules and enforcement actions that have targeted it. The law and enforcement data comes from the Leiser, Santos & Doshi 2023 database. Hard to cancel has by far the most real-world examples, and sneaking and forced action have the most enforcement actions.

key_items.name: Hard to cancel
key_items.one_line: Signing up is easy and leaving is deliberately difficult.
key_items.use_when: Reviewing any subscription, account deletion or opt-out flow

key_items.name: Preselection
key_items.one_line: The option that benefits the business is ticked or selected by default.
key_items.use_when: Reviewing forms, consent screens and checkout add-ons

key_items.name: Sneaking / hidden costs / hidden subscription
key_items.one_line: Material facts such as price, recurring charges or extra items are hidden or held back until late in the flow.

key_items.name: Confirmshaming / nagging / fake urgency / fake scarcity / fake social proof
key_items.one_line: Emotional pressure, repeated interruptions, or invented time, stock or popularity cues.

key_items.name: Trick wording / visual interference / disguised ads / comparison prevention
key_items.one_line: Language or layout that misleads, hides information, or makes options hard to compare.

sources.name: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (FTC Staff Report, September 2022)
sources.publisher: US Federal Trade Commission, Bureau of Consumer Protection
sources.license: Public domain (US Government work), but only per the FTC Website Policy as indexed by anysearch. The policy page body could not be read directly (bot wall), so this is unconfirmed.
sources.version_or_date: September 2022 (follows the 29 April 2021 workshop)
sources.summary: The US regulator's staff report on dark patterns. It defines them as design practices that trick or manipulate people into choices they would not otherwise make and that may cause harm. It ties common patterns to FTC enforcement cases and gives recommendations for companies. It stresses that patterns stack: combined patterns hit harder than single ones. One study it cites found that dark patterns doubled sign-ups for a dubious service compared with a neutral interface.

key_items.name: Definition
key_items.one_line: Design practices that trick or manipulate users into choices they would not otherwise make and that may cause harm.
key_items.use_when: Setting the audit bar in a deceptive-pattern review

key_items.name: Compounding effect
key_items.one_line: Several patterns used together do more harm than any one alone, so audit whole flows, not single screens.

sources.name: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces (v2.0)
sources.license: EDPB reuse policy (not Creative Commons): reuse allowed for commercial and non-commercial purposes if the source is acknowledged
sources.version_or_date: Version 2.0, adopted 14 February 2023 (final version published 24 February 2023)
sources.summary: GDPR-grounded guidance on recognising and avoiding deceptive interface patterns. It sorts them into six categories with 16 named sub-types in all (my count). It recommends that interdisciplinary teams assess interfaces across the whole account lifecycle, from sign-up to deletion. Written for social media but easy to apply to any consent or privacy UI.

key_items.name: Overloading
key_items.one_line: Bury the user in requests, information or options so they share more data (continuous prompting, privacy maze, too many options).

key_items.name: Skipping
key_items.one_line: Design the journey so users forget about data protection (deceptive snugness, look over there).

key_items.name: Stirring
key_items.one_line: Steer choices through emotion or visual nudges (emotional steering, hidden in plain sight).

key_items.name: Obstructing
key_items.one_line: Make getting informed or managing data hard or impossible (dead end, longer than necessary, misleading action).

key_items.name: Fickle
key_items.one_line: Inconsistent, unclear interfaces that make privacy controls hard to find (lacking hierarchy, decontextualising, inconsistent interface, language discontinuity).

key_items.name: Left in the dark
key_items.one_line: Hide information or controls, or leave users unsure how their data is used (conflicting information, ambiguous wording).

sources.publisher: Princeton University Web Transparency & Accountability Project

sources.summary: A large crawl-based measurement study. Across about 53K product pages on about 11K shopping sites it found 1,818 dark-pattern instances of 15 types, on about 11% of the sites. sources.license: Open Government Licence v3.0
sources.version_or_date: Live page read 2026-10-15
sources.summary: Content-design rules for transactional UI copy. If the interface needs explaining, fix the interface. Keep help text and labels short. Skip apologies and jokes in error messages, because people use these services under stress. Never refer to things by colour or position. Every input must have a question tied to it in the markup. key_items.one_line: Needing to explain how the interface works is a sign it is broken.

key_items.name: Error tone
key_items.one_line: No 'sorry' and no humour in validation errors; say what went wrong and how to fix it.

key_items.name: No sensory references
key_items.one_line: Do not tell users to 'click the green button'.

sources.summary: Sample-size rule for open card sorts in IA work. 5 users correlate only about 0.75 with the eventual result, 15 users reach about 0.90 (the recommended stopping point), and 30 reach about 0.95, which is only worth it for big, well-funded projects. key_items.one_line: Run at least 15 participants per card sort; it takes 3 times the usual 5-user test to stabilise similarity scores.

key_items.name: Generative then evaluative
key_items.one_line: Use the sort to set direction, then test a drafted structure with users.

sources.license: Apache-2.0 (carbon-design-system/carbon-website repo; site footer copyright 2026 IBM)
sources.version_or_date: Live 2026 (repo pushed 2026-09-30)
sources.summary: A token-based motion system with two styles. Productive motion is quick and subtle, for task flow and micro-interactions. Expressive motion is held back for occasional important moments. Durations are named tokens from fast-01 (70ms) to slow-02 (700ms), easing curves are packaged, and a checklist asks whether micro-interactions stay in the 90-120ms range. Apache-2.0, so it can be vendored.

key_items.name: Productive vs expressive
key_items.one_line: Default to productive; spend expressive motion only on important moments.

key_items.name: Duration tokens
key_items.one_line: fast-01 70ms, fast-02 110ms, moderate-01 150ms, moderate-02 240ms, slow-01 400ms, slow-02 700ms.

sources.name: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions
sources.license: W3C Software and Document License (permissive)
sources.version_or_date: WCAG 2.2; Level AAA
sources.summary: Users must be able to turn off motion triggered by their own interaction unless the motion is essential. The page explains vestibular harm such as dizziness, nausea and migraine, and names parallax as a common offender. Sufficient techniques include honouring the prefers-reduced-motion media query in CSS (C39) or JS (SCR40). It is AAA, so it is advisory unless the project targets AAA, but it is the right default for a motion principle.

key_items.name: C39 / SCR40
key_items.one_line: Honour prefers-reduced-motion in CSS or script to drop non-essential motion.

key_items.name: 2.2.2 vs 2.3.3
key_items.one_line: Auto-started motion falls under 2.2.2 (Level A); interaction-triggered motion falls under 2.3.3.

sources.summary: Government chart guidance. It matches chart type to data relationship and asks for clear labels, direct labelling of series rather than legends, and not relying on colour alone. Numerical axes should start at zero (use a dot plot if that hides the story), pie charts should have at most five categories, 3D should be avoided, and charts need accessible titles and alt text. OGL, so it can be vendored with attribution. This fills the data-viz gap.

key_items.name: Axis and labels
key_items.one_line: Start bar axes at zero, label directly, never encode meaning only in colour.

sources.summary: The baseline i18n checklist. Use UTF-8 everywhere, declare the language and mark changes of language, and support local formats for names, addresses and dates. Make navigation to localised versions visible. For RTL, set dir on the root and change it only where the base direction changes, use logical start/end rather than left/right, and wrap opposite-direction phrases inline. Also be careful with text inside images that will be translated. This fills the localisation/RTL gap.

sources.summary: A four-phase lifecycle: Proposal (public discussion, at least 45 days of comment), Development, Released (with a 'use with caution' state when a component fails accessibility, usability or development requirements), and Deprecated (kept in the code base, no longer updated, removal recommended). mapping_ideas: new-playbook:deceptive-pattern-audit - Walk every flow (sign-up, checkout, consent, cancel, delete). Tag each finding with a deceptive.design type AND an EDPB category, attach a screenshot, name the legal hook (DSA Art. 25, GDPR via EDPB, FTC, ICO code), rate severity, and propose the honest alternative. Treat stacked patterns in one flow as more severe. Grounded in deceptive.design, EDPB 03/2022 v2.0, FTC 2022, DSA Art. 25, Mathur 2019.

new-principle:symmetry-of-choice - Cancelling takes no more steps than subscribing, accept and reject get equal prominence, nothing that benefits the business is preselected, and a choice already made is not asked again. Grounded in DSA Art. 25(3)(a)-(c) and the deceptive.design hard-to-cancel and preselection types. This is the UI form of make-operations-idempotent and design-for-reversal.

new-principle:pin-the-legal-target (extend the accessibility angle's version to ethics and privacy) - In discovery, record which ethics and privacy regimes apply (EU DSA, GDPR per EDPB, UK ICO Children's code, US FTC) and write them into the todo list as gates. Grounded in DSA Art. 25, EDPB, ICO, FTC.

new-principle:child-best-interest-by-default - If under-18s are likely users, default to high privacy, ban privacy-weakening nudges, and write transparency copy for their age. Grounded in the ICO Age appropriate design code (OGL, vendorable).

new-playbook:content-design-pass - Start from a written user-need statement, then draft labels, questions, hints and errors (no 'sorry', no humour, no colour or position references, one question per input). Run a plain-language check and a voice-and-tone check. Grounded in GOV.UK Writing for UIs and Understand content design (OGL), Digital.gov plain-language guides (CC0), and Mailchimp (link only, NC). Design form of principle:minimize-reader-load and skill:technical-writing.
new-principle:fix-the-ui-not-the-help-text - If the copy has to explain the interface, change the interface. Grounded in GOV.UK Writing for UIs. Pairs with principle:subtract-before-you-add.

new-playbook:ia-validation - The agent prepares an open card-sort kit (cards from real content and research nouns, at least 15 participants per user group, screener, consent), then a tree-test kit for the drafted structure. A human runs the sessions, and the agent analyses similarity matrices and success paths. Never simulate participants. Grounded in NN/g card-sort sizing. Pairs with playbook:object-mapping (OOUX).

new-playbook:service-blueprint - For any multi-channel or staff-assisted journey, map customer actions, frontstage, backstage, support processes and evidence per touchpoint, then mark failpoints, wait points and redundant data entry. Grounded in NN/g Service Blueprints. Concrete form of principle:solve-the-whole-problem and principle:model-the-domain.

new-playbook:ai-feature-design - For any AI or agentic feature: first ask whether AI is needed at all (PAIR user needs), then go through the 18 HAX guidelines by phase (initially, during use, when wrong, over time), writing a decision or N/A with a rationale for each, and specify onboarding, explanation, feedback controls and graceful failure states. Grounded in Microsoft HAX (license unknown, link only) and Google PAIR (CC BY-NC-SA, link only).

new-principle:design-for-ai-being-wrong - No AI feature ships without specified dismiss, correct and undo paths and an explanation of why it acted. Grounded in HAX 'when wrong' and the PAIR errors + graceful failure chapter. AI form of principle:fix-root-causes and design-for-reversal.

new-principle:motion-has-a-job - Every animation states its purpose. Productive motion is the default; expressive motion is rationed (pairs with spend-boldness-once). Durations come from tokens, and prefers-reduced-motion is honoured even when AAA is not the target. Grounded in Carbon Motion (Apache-2.0), WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.3 + C39, WSG 2.10.

new-playbook:chart-review - Pick the chart by data relationship, label series directly, start bar axes at zero (or switch to a dot plot), allow at most five pie categories, use no 3D and never colour alone, and write accessible titles and alt text. Report findings with the rule cited. Grounded in the Government Analysis Function charts guidance (OGL, vendorable). Complements the installed dataviz skill and principle:explain-the-number.

new-playbook:i18n-rtl-readiness - Check lang and dir declarations, use logical properties over left/right, isolate bidi text inline, and allow for text expansion and local name/address/date formats. Pseudo-localise and render an RTL screenshot pass before handoff. Grounded in W3C i18n Quick Tips and Authoring HTML: Handling RTL (W3C license). Feeds principle:worst-case-content.

new-principle:sustainable-by-default - Use the WSG Section 2 UX guidelines as an advisory lens (efficient journeys, no unwanted notifications, proportionate media and animation, design-system reuse). Label it as a draft Note and never as a gate. Grounded in W3C WSG Group Note Draft 2026-09-24. Reinforces subtract-before-you-add and normative-over-draft.

new-playbook:design-critique-ritual - Before review, write down the agreed objectives and users. Then run a facilitated multi-agent critique: one facilitator agent, N reviewer agents with fixed quotas of strengths and issues, findings stated as problems against objectives, never taste. Grounded in NN/g Design Critiques. This is how skill:arena and skill:interrogate apply to design.

new-playbook:maturity-retro - At the measure stage, score the team on the NN/g 6 UX maturity stages (link only) and the W3C AMM (from the a11y angle). Turn each recurring gap into a design-system rule, lint or template. Grounded in NN/g UX maturity and W3C AMM. Feeds principle:encode-lessons-in-structure.

principle:migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis -> deprecate-through-a-lifecycle - Mark the component 'use with caution', publish its replacement, migrate every screen that uses it, mark it deprecated (still available, no updates), and only then remove it. Grounded in the USWDS component lifecycle (CC0).

pstack coverage, real design analogs that need no new research: minimize-reader-load -> content-design-pass; build-the-lever and type-system-discipline -> DTCG-typed tokens and token-pipeline (design-systems angle); make-operations-idempotent -> design-for-reversal + symmetry-of-choice; sequence-verifiable-units and playbook:hillclimb -> iterative 5-user rounds (research-validation angle; the RITE method itself is an open gap); playbook:trace-forensics and runtime-forensics -> analytics/funnel forensics against a HEART metrics plan; playbook:eval -> rubric-scored design evals (heuristic severity, SUS/SEQ norms); laziness-protocol -> reuse an existing design-system pattern before designing a new one (GOV.UK contribution criteria); boundary-discipline -> component API/props and slot contracts; workflow skill:tdd -> write usability acceptance criteria before designing; skill:unslop -> Impeccable anti-slop detector; skill:reflect -> maturity-retro.
